Basics of Derivatives.overview: This chapter introduces what derivatives are, how their value depends on an underlying asset, and the main types: forwards, futures, options and swaps. It contrasts exchange-traded and OTC contracts, explains the roles of hedgers, speculators and arbitrageurs, and covers the economic functions of derivatives such as price discovery and risk transfer. When revising, be clear on counterparty risk, standardisation, leverage and why derivatives markets attract both risk managers and traders. Expect conceptual questions with short scenarios.
questions: Which of the following is an example of a derivative whose underlying is not a financial asset?
An equity share of an oil company
A Treasury Bill issued by the RBI
A futures contract on crude oil
A unit of a liquid mutual fund scheme
A crude oil future derives its value from a physical commodity. An equity share, a T-Bill and a mutual fund unit are themselves primary securities, not contracts deriving value from something else.
A jeweller expects to buy gold in three months and fears a price rise. Using derivatives, she is acting as a hedger if she:
Sells gold futures to profit from an expected fall
Buys gold futures to lock in her purchase cost
Buys gold futures purely because she expects prices to rise
Buys gold in one market and sells it in another at the same time

A hedger uses derivatives to offset an existing or expected exposure. Buying futures fixes the cost of a future purchase. Taking a view without exposure is speculation, and simultaneous buy-sell for a price gap is arbitrage.
Why are swaps generally classified as OTC derivatives rather than exchange-traded ones?
They can be traded only by the Reserve Bank of India
They never involve exchange of any cash flows between parties
They are always settled by physical delivery of the underlying
Their terms are privately negotiated between two parties

Swaps are bilateral agreements whose notional, tenor and payment terms are tailored to the parties' needs, which is the hallmark of OTC contracts. They do involve exchange of cash flows, usually net, not physical delivery.
What does 'leverage' in a futures position mean for a trader?
A small margin controls a large contract value
The trader pays the full contract value upfront and earns interest on it
Losses are capped at the margin deposited with the broker
The exchange guarantees a minimum return on every position

Futures require only a margin, a fraction of the contract value, so price changes on the full value produce large percentage gains or losses on capital. Losses are not capped at the margin; further mark-to-market calls can arise.
Price discovery as a function of derivatives markets refers to:
The exchange fixing the price of the underlying at the start of each month
Derivatives prices reflecting expectations about future spot prices
SEBI announcing a fair value for every listed derivatives contract
The issuer of the underlying deciding the price of its own futures

Active trading by many participants with different views makes derivatives prices reflect collective expectations about the underlying. Neither the exchange, SEBI nor the issuer sets these prices administratively.
An arbitrageur notices that a stock's futures price is well below its theoretical fair value. Which trade locks in a riskless profit, ignoring costs?
Buy the futures and sell the stock in the cash market
Buy the stock in the cash market and sell the futures
Buy both the stock and the futures together
Sell the futures and wait for the price to fall

When futures are cheap relative to fair value, the arbitrageur buys the underpriced futures and sells the relatively expensive spot, unwinding at expiry when prices converge. Buying spot and selling futures is the trade for overpriced futures.
Which risk is substantially lower in exchange-traded derivatives than in OTC derivatives, because of the clearing corporation?
Market price risk
Basis risk
Volatility risk
Counterparty default risk

The clearing corporation becomes the counterparty to every trade through novation and guarantees settlement, so default risk falls sharply. Market, basis and volatility risks come from price behaviour and remain regardless of where the contract trades.
A speculator differs from a hedger mainly because the speculator:
Always holds both the derivative and the underlying asset
Is prohibited from trading in exchange-traded derivatives
Takes on price risk without an exposure to protect
Uses only options and never trades futures contracts

Speculators take on risk in the hope of profiting from price movements; they do not have an underlying exposure to protect. They may use futures or options and are an important source of liquidity in exchange markets.

Understanding Index.overview: This chapter explains what a stock market index is, how it is constructed and maintained, and why it is used as an underlying for derivatives. Key topics are weighting methods (price-weighted, market-cap and free-float weighted), base value and base period, index maintenance for corporate actions, impact cost and the attributes of a good index. Revise how free-float market cap is computed, why index divisors change, and the uses of indices such as benchmarking, index funds, ETFs and index derivatives.
questions: A company has total market capitalisation of ₹40,000 crore and its promoters hold 60% of the shares. If all other shares are free-float, what is its free-float market capitalisation?
₹24,000 crore
₹16,000 crore
₹40,000 crore
₹10,000 crore

Free float excludes promoter holding, so the free-float portion is 40% of shares. Free-float market cap = 40% × ₹40,000 crore = ₹16,000 crore. ₹24,000 crore is the promoter portion, not the free float.
When a constituent stock of a market-cap weighted index is replaced by another stock, the index provider adjusts the divisor so that:
The index value is reset to its original base value
The new stock gets the same weight as the stock it replaced
The index value rises by the new stock's market capitalisation
The index value does not change merely because of the replacement

Divisor adjustments keep the index continuous so that only market price movements, not changes in composition or corporate actions, change the index level. Weights still depend on each stock's own free-float market cap.
In a price-weighted index, which stock has the greatest influence on index movements?
The stock with the highest share price
The stock with the largest market capitalisation
The stock with the highest trading volume
The stock with the most free-float shares

In a price-weighted index, each stock's weight depends on its price, so high-priced shares move the index most regardless of company size. Market-cap based indices instead give larger companies more weight.
Which corporate action normally requires an index divisor adjustment in a free-float market-cap index?
A normal daily rise in the price of a constituent
A change in the company's statutory auditor
A rights issue by a constituent company
A constituent's announcement of quarterly results

A rights issue changes the share count and hence market cap without a pure price move, so the divisor is adjusted to keep the index continuous. Daily price changes are what the index is meant to capture.
An index fund manager's portfolio returned 11.4% while the benchmark index returned 12.0%. The 0.6% difference is best described as:
Alpha generated by superior stock selection
Tracking difference due to costs
Impact cost of the index constituents
Basis between the index and its futures

An index fund aims to match its benchmark; the gap between fund and index return is tracking difference, caused by expenses, cash holdings and replication lags. It is negative here, so it is not alpha.
Lower impact cost for the stocks in an index is desirable for derivatives trading mainly because it:
Guarantees that the index will rise over time
Reduces the number of stocks needed in the index
Makes index arbitrage and hedging cheaper to execute
Removes the need for margins on index futures

Low impact cost means large trades in the constituents can be executed close to quoted prices, so arbitrageurs and hedgers can replicate the index cheaply. This keeps futures prices close to fair value.
An index had a base value of 1,000 and its current free-float market cap is 25 times the base-period free-float market cap. Ignoring divisor adjustments, the index value is:
Index value = base value × (current market cap ÷ base market cap) = 1,000 × 25 = 25,000. The ratio of market caps is applied multiplicatively to the base value, not added to it.
Which of these is NOT a common use of a stock market index?
Benchmarking the performance of fund managers
Serving as the underlying for index futures and options
Creating index funds and exchange-traded funds
Fixing the issue price of a company's IPO

Indices are used to benchmark portfolios, as underlyings for derivatives and as the basis for passive products. IPO prices are discovered through book building or fixed by the issuer with the lead manager, not by an index.

Introduction to Forwards and Futures.overview: This chapter covers forward and futures contracts: their features, differences, payoff profiles and pricing. Learn the cost-of-carry model, the effect of dividends and interest on fair value, basis and convergence, contango and backwardation, mark-to-market settlement and the use of futures for hedging with beta. Practise numerical questions on fair value, implied interest rates, daily mark-to-market and hedge ratios, and be clear about how stock and index futures are settled in India.
questions: A stock trades at ₹1,000 and its two-month futures trade at ₹1,012. Ignoring dividends, what annualised simple interest rate is implied in the futures price?
7.2% per annum
1.2% per annum
6.0% per annum
14.4% per annum
Implied two-month return = 12 ÷ 1,000 = 1.2%. Annualised simply, 1.2% × 12/2 = 7.2% per annum. 1.2% is the unannualised figure; 14.4% wrongly annualises by multiplying by 12.
A trader is long futures on 250 shares bought at ₹820. Settlement prices are ₹832 on day 1 and ₹815 on day 2. What is the mark-to-market amount on day 2?
Loss of ₹1,250
Gain of ₹3,000
Loss of ₹4,250
Loss of ₹1,750

Day 2 MTM compares the day 2 settlement price with the day 1 settlement price: (815 − 832) × 250 = −₹4,250. The cumulative loss from the purchase price is ₹1,250, but that is not the day 2 MTM figure.
Other things equal, if a stock is expected to pay a large dividend before the futures expiry, the fair futures price will be:
Higher than it would be without the dividend
Lower than it would be without the dividend
Exactly equal to the spot price
Unaffected, because dividends go to the futures buyer

In the cost-of-carry model, income from holding the underlying reduces the carry, so fair value = spot + interest − dividends. A futures buyer does not receive the dividend, so the futures price adjusts down.
Which feature is found in forward contracts but not in exchange-traded futures?
Daily mark-to-market settlement through a clearing corporation
Standardised lot sizes and expiry dates
Guarantee of performance by a clearing corporation
Terms such as quantity and delivery date tailored to the two parties

Forwards are private, customised agreements. Futures are standardised exchange contracts with daily mark-to-market and a clearing corporation guarantee, which is why futures carry far less counterparty risk.
A portfolio manager holds equity worth ₹5 crore with beta 0.9 and wants to hedge fully using index futures. Each contract has a value of ₹15 lakh. Approximately how many contracts should she sell?
33 contracts
27 contracts
36 contracts
30 contracts
Contracts = portfolio value × beta ÷ contract value = 5,00,00,000 × 0.9 ÷ 15,00,000 = 30. Ignoring beta gives about 33, which would over-hedge a portfolio that is less volatile than the index.
At expiry of a futures contract, the futures price and spot price of the underlying:
Diverge by the full cost of carry
Converge, so the basis becomes approximately zero
Remain apart by the amount of the initial margin
Differ by the dividend expected next year
As time to expiry shrinks, the cost of carry falls to zero, so the futures price converges to the spot price and the basis disappears. Arbitrage ensures this convergence on the final settlement day.
An investor holding a stock portfolio sells index futures equal to its beta-adjusted value. If the market falls 5%, the hedge is intended to:
Offset portfolio losses with gains on the short futures
Double the gain made on the portfolio
Convert the whole portfolio into a risk-free bond paying 5%
Eliminate company-specific risk in the stocks held
A short index futures hedge gains when the market falls, offsetting the market-related loss on the portfolio. It removes systematic exposure only; stock-specific risk not explained by beta remains.
A trader buys Nifty futures and holds them overnight. The next day, the settlement price falls. What happens to his account?
Nothing happens until he closes the position
His initial margin is refunded and the position is closed
His account is debited with the mark-to-market loss for the day
He receives the dividend on index stocks to offset the loss

Futures positions are marked to market daily: losses are debited and gains credited based on the daily settlement price. The position remains open unless he squares it off or fails to meet margin requirements.

Introduction to Options.overview: This chapter introduces call and put options, option terminology (strike, premium, expiry, moneyness), payoffs for buyers and sellers, intrinsic and time value, put-call parity, and option pricing models such as Black-Scholes and binomial. It also covers the option Greeks: delta, gamma, theta, vega and rho. When revising, practise payoff and break-even calculations, understand how volatility and time affect premiums, and know how Greeks are used to manage option positions.
questions: A stock trades at ₹1,240 and a call option with a strike of ₹1,200 is priced at ₹62. What is the time value of the option?
Intrinsic value of the call = 1,240 − 1,200 = ₹40. Time value = premium − intrinsic value = 62 − 40 = ₹22. ₹40 is the intrinsic value, not the time value.
A trader holds long call options covering 2,000 shares, each with a delta of 0.6. To make the position delta neutral, he should:
Sell 1,200 shares of the underlying
Buy 1,200 shares of the underlying
Sell 2,000 shares of the underlying
Buy 800 shares of the underlying
Position delta = 2,000 × 0.6 = +1,200 share-equivalents. To neutralise it, he must sell 1,200 shares. Buying would increase the delta, and selling 2,000 shares would over-hedge.
A put option with a strike of ₹500 is said to be out of the money when the underlying stock price is:
A put is out of the money when the spot price is above the strike, since exercising would mean selling below market. At ₹470 or ₹450 the put is in the money, and at ₹500 it is at the money.
Which option position has a gain potential limited to the premium received but a potentially large loss?
Long put
Short put
Long call
Long straddle
A put writer earns at most the premium, while losses grow as the stock falls, up to the strike minus premium. Long option positions risk only the premium paid and have large profit potential.
Just before an important company announcement, implied volatility on its options rises sharply. Other things equal, this will:
Increase the premiums of both calls and puts
Increase call premiums but reduce put premiums
Reduce the premiums of both calls and puts
Leave premiums unchanged because the stock price has not moved

Higher volatility raises the probability of large moves in either direction, increasing the value of both calls and puts. This sensitivity to volatility is measured by vega, which is positive for long calls and long puts.
Gamma of an option is usually highest when the option is:
Deep out of the money with long time to expiry
Deep in the money with long time to expiry
At the money and close to expiry
Far out of the money and close to expiry

Gamma measures how fast delta changes. Near-the-money options close to expiry have deltas that swing sharply between 0 and 1 for small price moves, so their gamma peaks. Deep ITM or OTM options have stable deltas.
A call buyer pays a premium of ₹45 for a strike of ₹1,500. Ignoring costs, at what expiry price does he break even?
For a long call, break-even = strike + premium = 1,500 + 45 = ₹1,545. Above this level he makes a net profit. ₹1,455 would be the break-even for a long put with the same strike and premium.
In the Black-Scholes model, which input is NOT directly observable in the market and must be estimated?
Current price of the underlying
Volatility of the underlying's returns
Strike price of the option
Time remaining to expiry

Spot price, strike and time to expiry are known. Volatility must be estimated, either historically or by backing it out of market prices as implied volatility, which is why it is the key uncertain input.

Strategies using Equity Futures and Opti.overview: This chapter applies futures and options to trading and hedging. It covers directional trades, hedging with futures, protective puts and covered calls, spreads (bull, bear, calendar), straddles, strangles, butterflies and collars, and arbitrage strategies. Revise each strategy's market view, maximum profit, maximum loss and break-even points. Many exam questions ask you to choose a strategy for a given view on direction and volatility, or to compute payoffs, so practise drawing simple payoff tables.
questions: A trader buys a ₹1,000 call at ₹30 and sells a ₹1,050 call at ₹12, same stock and expiry. What is his maximum profit per share?
Net debit = 30 − 12 = ₹18. Maximum profit = difference in strikes − net debit = 50 − 18 = ₹32, earned if the stock ends at or above ₹1,050. ₹18 is the maximum loss, not the profit.
A trader buys a ₹500 call at ₹20 and a ₹500 put at ₹18, same expiry. What are his break-even prices at expiry?
Total premium = 20 + 18 = ₹38. Break-evens of a long straddle are strike ± total premium: 500 − 38 = ₹462 and 500 + 38 = ₹538. Using only one leg's premium gives the wrong figures.
An investor expects a stock to fall modestly but wants to limit the cost of the position. Which strategy suits this view best?
Long straddle
Bear put spread
Bull call spread
Short strangle

A bear put spread (buy higher-strike put, sell lower-strike put) profits from a moderate fall at lower cost than a single put. A straddle bets on volatility, a bull spread on a rise, and a short strangle on a quiet market.
A calendar spread using calls typically involves:
Selling a near-month and buying a far-month call, same strike
Buying and selling calls of different strikes in the same month
Buying a call and a put of the same strike and month
Selling calls on two different underlying stocks

A calendar (time) spread uses the same strike but different expiries, aiming to profit from faster time decay in the near-month option. Different strikes in the same month form a vertical spread, not a calendar spread.
An investor owns shares at ₹400, buys a ₹380 put for ₹8 and sells a ₹440 call for ₹8. Ignoring costs, what is his maximum loss per share?
This zero-cost collar has a net premium of nil. If the stock falls below ₹380, the put lets him sell at ₹380, so maximum loss = 400 − 380 = ₹20. Gains are capped at ₹40 by the short call.
Which strategy profits most if the underlying ends exactly at the middle strike at expiry?
Long strangle
Protective put
Long butterfly spread
Short futures

A long butterfly (buy one low strike, sell two middle strikes, buy one high strike) has its peak payoff at the middle strike. A long strangle needs a large move, a protective put protects against falls, and short futures profits from falls.
A trader sells a ₹2,000 put and receives ₹35. He is effectively:
Protecting a stock he already owns from a fall
Betting on a large rise in the stock's implied volatility
Locking in a sale price of ₹2,035 for his shares
Ready to buy the stock at a net ₹1,965 if assigned
If the stock falls below ₹2,000, the put writer must buy at ₹2,000, but the ₹35 premium lowers the effective cost to ₹1,965. Selling puts is a bullish-to-neutral, short-volatility position.
Short selling a stock's futures while buying the stock in the cash market, when futures are overpriced, is known as:
Reverse cash-and-carry arbitrage
Cash-and-carry arbitrage
Calendar spread trading
Pair trading
In cash-and-carry arbitrage, the trader buys the spot, sells the expensive futures and holds until expiry, earning more than the financing cost. Reverse cash-and-carry is used when futures are cheap.

Trading Mechanism.overview: This chapter explains how equity derivatives are traded on Indian exchanges: the electronic order-matching system, types of orders, contract specifications, lot sizes, expiry rules, price bands, position limits, the market-wide position limit and ban period, and the roles of trading members, clearing members and clients. Revise order types and conditions, how open interest changes with trades, the meaning of the F&O ban period, and the eligibility criteria for stocks in the derivatives segment.
questions: A trader places an order that must be executed immediately in full or partially, with any unexecuted part cancelled at once. This is an:
Good Till Cancelled order
Stop-loss order
Immediate or Cancel (IOC) order
Day order

An IOC order executes whatever quantity is available immediately and cancels the rest. A day order stays in the book till the end of the day, and a stop-loss order activates only when a trigger price is reached.
During the ban period for a stock in the F&O segment, a trader with an existing long futures position can:
Freely increase the position
Only reduce the position, not increase it
Neither reduce nor increase the position
Convert it into an options position at no cost

When a stock's open interest crosses the market-wide position limit, it enters the ban period: fresh positions that increase exposure are not allowed, but existing positions can be reduced or closed. Breaching this attracts penalties.
Trades in the equity derivatives segment of NSE are matched on the basis of:
Size of order only
Alphabetical order of member codes
Random selection by the system
Price-time priority
The order-matching system gives priority first to the best price and, at the same price, to the order entered earlier. This transparent rule applies to all members and ensures fair execution.
Two traders both close out existing positions against each other: one sells to close a long, the other buys to close a short. Open interest will:
Decrease
Increase
Remain unchanged
Double
Open interest counts outstanding contracts. When both sides are closing existing positions, one contract is extinguished, so open interest falls. If both were opening new positions, it would rise.
Which entity places orders on the exchange trading system on behalf of clients?
A trading member
The clearing corporation
The depository participant
The registrar and share transfer agent
Trading members (brokers) are authorised to enter orders on the exchange. The clearing corporation clears and settles trades, depositories hold securities, and RTAs handle issuer registers.
A trader places a sell order with a trigger price of ₹490 and a limit price of ₹488 on a stock futures contract trading at ₹500. This order will:
Be executed immediately at ₹500
Be executed only if the futures price first rises back up to ₹490
Activate at ₹490, then sell at ₹488 or better
Sell at any price once the market opens
A stop-loss sell order lies dormant until the trigger is hit. Once the price falls to ₹490, it becomes a limit order to sell at ₹488 or higher, protecting the trader from further losses.
Why are stocks admitted to the derivatives segment required to meet criteria on liquidity, market cap and trading volume?
To guarantee that those stocks will give positive returns
To limit derivatives trading to government-owned companies
To ensure that each stock pays regular dividends
To ensure the underlying is liquid and hard to manipulate
Eligibility norms ensure the underlying cash market is deep and widely traded, making price manipulation harder and arbitrage and hedging feasible. They say nothing about future returns or dividends.
A client wants to trade equity derivatives through a broker. Which of the following is mandatory before trading?
Depositing the full contract value of every trade with the exchange
Completing KYC and signing the required risk disclosure documents
Obtaining a separate registration from SEBI as a derivatives trader
Holding at least ₹10 lakh of shares in a demat account

Clients must complete KYC and receive risk disclosure documents and rights and obligations before trading derivatives. They pay margins, not full contract value, and need no separate SEBI registration.

Clearing and Settlement System.overview: This chapter covers how equity derivatives trades are cleared and settled: the role of the clearing corporation and clearing members, novation, determination of obligations, mark-to-market and final settlement, exercise and assignment of options, and the risk management system. Revise SPAN-style initial margin, exposure margin, premium margin, assignment margin, the settlement guarantee fund, client margin collection and how positions are closed out. Expect questions on who pays which margin and how settlement differs for futures, options, index and stock contracts.
questions: A trader is short a stock call option and it is exercised at expiry. Which process determines that he must fulfil the obligation?
Novation by the trading member
Exercise by the option seller
Assignment by the clearing corporation
Netting by the depository
When long option holders exercise, the clearing corporation randomly assigns the obligation to short positions. Exercise is the buyer's right; assignment is how sellers are chosen to meet it.
An option buyer pays the premium on the trade. When is the premium normally settled under current Indian practice?
Upfront, at the time of the trade
Only at expiry, if the option is exercised
Daily, as mark-to-market on the option's value
It is never paid if the option expires worthless
Option buyers must pay the premium upfront; brokers collect it before or at the time of the trade. Options are not marked to market daily like futures; the buyer's maximum loss is this premium.
Initial margin in the equity derivatives segment is designed to cover:
The full contract value of the position, payable on the trade date
Potential one-day losses on a position under adverse price and volatility scenarios
The brokerage and taxes payable on the trade
Losses arising only on the expiry day
Initial margin is set using a risk-based model that estimates the largest likely one-day loss under various scenarios. It is a fraction of contract value, sized to protect the clearing corporation.
If a clearing member fails to meet its settlement obligation, the first resource the clearing corporation uses is typically:
The Core Settlement Guarantee Fund
Contributions from non-defaulting clients
A loan from the Reserve Bank of India
The defaulting member's own margins and collateral
In the default waterfall, the defaulter's margins and deposits are used first. Only if these are insufficient does the clearing corporation draw on the settlement guarantee fund and other resources.
A professional clearing member (PCM) in the derivatives segment:
Trades only on its own account and clears its own trades
Acts as a depository that holds all derivatives positions of clients
Clears trades of trading members but does not trade itself
Is a type of client that uses multiple brokers
A PCM is a clearing-only entity, often a bank or custodian, that clears and settles trades executed by trading members or custodial participants. It does not have trading rights of its own.
Final settlement of stock futures that remain open at expiry in India is done by:
Cash settlement at the closing price of the index
Physical delivery of the underlying shares
Rolling over automatically to the next month
Cancellation without any settlement

Stock futures and stock options open at expiry are physically settled: the long receives shares and pays the settlement value. Index derivatives are cash settled because the index cannot be delivered.
Why do brokers collect margins from clients upfront rather than after the trade?
Exchange rules require it and penalise short collection
Clients can only pay margins after their trades make a profit
Margins are a fee paid to the broker for executing trades
Upfront margins are collected only from institutional clients
SEBI and exchange norms require brokers to collect initial margins from clients before trading, and short or non-collection attracts penalties on the member. Margins are collateral, not fees.
A trader's short option position faces a sharp rise in volatility. Which margin is most likely to increase?
The premium paid on his long option positions
The settlement guarantee fund contribution of the exchange
The stamp duty on the contract
Initial margin on the short option
Risk-based initial margins on short options rise when volatility increases, since potential losses widen. Premiums on longs are already paid, and stamp duty does not depend on volatility.

Legal and Regulatory Environment.overview: This chapter covers the legal framework for equity derivatives in India: the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, the SEBI Act, 1992, the Depositories Act, SEBI regulations for stock brokers and the role of SEBI and exchanges. It also covers the evolution of derivatives regulation, position limits, measures to curb excessive speculation and rules against market abuse. Focus on which law defines derivatives, which body approves contracts and what position limits and surveillance measures aim to achieve.
questions: Which law gives SEBI the power to regulate the business in stock exchanges and protect investors' interests?
The Banking Regulation Act, 1949
The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
The Indian Contract Act, 1872
The Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992

The SEBI Act, 1992 established SEBI and gives it powers to regulate securities markets and protect investors. The Banking Regulation Act concerns banks, FEMA concerns foreign exchange, and the Contract Act covers general contracts.
A broker repeatedly places buy and sell orders between related accounts to create a false appearance of trading activity in a stock option. This is prohibited under:
SEBI's regulations governing the operations of mutual funds
SEBI's PFUTP regulations on fraudulent trade practices
The Companies Act provisions on share buyback
The RBI's guidelines on call money market
Creating artificial volume through circular or synthetic trades is a manipulative practice under SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations. It misleads other participants and attracts penalties and debarment.
Which body grants approval for a stock exchange to start trading in a new type of derivatives contract?
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs
The Reserve Bank of India
SEBI
The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India
Stock exchanges need SEBI's approval to introduce derivative products. MCA administers company law, RBI governs money and forex markets, and ICAI regulates accountants.
Position limits at the client level in equity derivatives aim mainly to:
Stop any one client from building a price-distorting position
Ensure that every client makes a profit
Fix a minimum number of contracts a client must trade
Restrict derivatives trading to large institutional investors only
Client-level limits cap concentration, reducing the risk of manipulation and of large defaults. They do not guarantee profits, set minimum trading or bar retail clients.
Under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, derivatives traded on recognised stock exchanges are:
Included within the definition of 'securities'
Excluded from the definition of 'securities'
Treated as bank deposits
Classified as insurance contracts
The SCRA was amended to include derivatives in the definition of securities, making exchange trading in derivatives legal and bringing them under SEBI's regulatory oversight.
A stock broker in the derivatives segment must maintain client funds:
In its own proprietary account to earn interest
In any bank account it chooses, as long as the client is informed later
With the clearing corporation only on expiry days
Separately, using them only for that client's obligations
SEBI requires segregation of client funds from the broker's own money; using one client's money for another client or for the broker's own trading is prohibited.
Which measure is designed by SEBI and exchanges to monitor and restrain excessive speculative positions in derivatives?
A fixed guaranteed return on every derivatives contract
Market-wide position limits and surveillance alerts
A ban on all retail clients from trading options
Compulsory physical delivery of index futures

Market-wide position limits, surveillance mechanisms and related measures monitor build-up of positions. They do not guarantee returns, ban retail clients outright, or require physical delivery of index contracts.
Disputes between a client and a trading member relating to derivatives trades can be resolved through:
The Reserve Bank's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme for banks
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority
The exchange's grievance cell and SEBI's ODR platform
The company whose shares are the underlying

Client complaints against brokers are handled through the exchange's grievance system, SCORES and the Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) platform with conciliation and arbitration. The banking ombudsman and IRDAI do not cover these disputes.

Accounting and Taxation.overview: This chapter covers how equity derivatives positions are accounted for and taxed in India. It includes accounting for initial margin, mark-to-market settlements, option premiums and open positions at year-end, and the tax treatment of F&O income as non-speculative business income, Securities Transaction Tax (STT), stamp duty and GST on charges. Rates change from time to time, so focus on concepts: what STT is levied on, who pays it, and how F&O profits and losses are classified and set off.
questions: Mark-to-market losses paid daily on an open futures position are accounted for by the client as:
A debit to a mark-to-market account
An increase in the value of shares held
A loan given to the clearing corporation
Revenue from operations

Daily MTM payments represent realised or notional changes in the value of the futures position and are recorded in an MTM account, which is closed to profit and loss on squaring off or at year-end per accounting standards.
For a resident individual, a loss from trading equity futures on a recognised exchange can generally be set off against:
Only salary income of the same year
Long-term capital gains of the next decade without limit
Agricultural income only
Other income except salary, in the same year

Exchange-traded F&O is treated as non-speculative business. Its loss can be set off against other heads except salary in the same year and carried forward against business income for up to eight years.
Securities Transaction Tax on an equity futures trade is levied on:
The buyer, on the margin amount paid
The seller, on the traded value of the futures contract
Both parties, on the brokerage paid
The clearing corporation, on open interest
STT on futures applies to the sell side on the traded value. It is not computed on margin or brokerage. The exact rate is notified in the Finance Act and has been revised from time to time.
An option buyer pays a premium of ₹20,000 and the option expires worthless. In the books, this premium is:
Carried forward as an asset indefinitely
Refunded by the clearing corporation
Written off as a loss in the profit and loss account
Added to the cost of shares in the portfolio
Option premium paid is shown as an asset while the position is open. If the option lapses unexercised, the premium has no remaining value and is charged to profit and loss as a loss.
Why is F&O trading on a recognised stock exchange treated differently from speculative business for tax purposes?
Because derivatives never involve any delivery of shares
Because SEBI collects income tax on F&O trades on behalf of the government
Because the law expressly excludes them from speculative transactions
Because all F&O profits are fully exempt from tax
Income-tax law expressly carves out eligible derivatives transactions on recognised exchanges from the speculative category, so they are non-speculative business. Profits are taxable, not exempt.
A trader who trades F&O as a business must maintain books and may require a tax audit when:
Statutory turnover or profit thresholds are met
He trades even a single option contract
His broker is located outside his city
He has made a profit in every month of the year

Tax audit applicability depends on statutory turnover and profit thresholds; F&O turnover is computed in a specific way. One contract alone does not trigger an audit, and location of the broker is irrelevant.
Stamp duty on equity derivatives trades in India is:
Paid by the seller to the stock exchange as a membership fee
Collected centrally through exchanges and paid by the buyer
Collected by SEBI as a regulatory fee
Not applicable to derivatives transactions at all
Under the amended Indian Stamp Act, stamp duty on securities transactions, including derivatives, is collected by exchanges or clearing corporations on behalf of states and is payable by the buyer.
Which accounting treatment applies to the initial margin deposited by a client with the broker?
It is booked as an expense in the year it is paid
It is shown as income of the client
It is treated as part of share capital
It is shown as a current asset, being recoverable
Initial margin is a deposit, not a cost, so it remains a current asset until returned. Only actual MTM losses, premiums lost and charges are expenses.

Sales Practices and Investor Protection.overview: This chapter covers responsible selling and investor protection in equity derivatives: assessing client suitability, risk disclosure, the code of conduct for brokers and their representatives, KYC, avoiding mis-selling, handling complaints, and the investor grievance redressal system including SCORES and online dispute resolution. It also covers investor protection funds and investor education. Revise what information must be given to clients, how to match products to client profiles and where an investor can escalate a grievance.
questions: A broker's representative tells a new client that a particular options strategy is 'risk-free and sure to earn 5% a month'. This is:
Acceptable if the client is experienced
Permitted when the strategy has worked in the past
A misleading statement that violates the code of conduct
Allowed if it is said orally and not in writing
Guaranteeing returns or describing leveraged options as risk-free misrepresents risk and breaches the broker code of conduct. No derivatives strategy can promise fixed monthly returns.
Before allowing a client to trade in derivatives, a broker should verify the client's:
Financial standing and risk-bearing ability
Political affiliation and religious views
Choice of mobile phone operator and internet provider
Preference between NSE and BSE indices
Brokers must gather information on income, net worth and experience to judge whether derivatives are appropriate. Unrelated personal details have no bearing on suitability.
An investor's complaint against a broker is not resolved satisfactorily. A next step available to him is to:
File the complaint with the Insurance Ombudsman
Approach the company whose shares he traded
Ask the Reserve Bank of India to reverse the disputed trade
Escalate on SCORES and use online dispute resolution
Securities market complaints can be lodged on SCORES and pursued through conciliation and arbitration on the ODR portal. Insurance ombudsman, the issuer company and RBI are not the right forums.
Why must brokers send contract notes to clients after derivatives trades?
To advertise new products to the client
To give a legal record of executed trades and charges
To request additional brokerage from the client
To inform the client of the next day's market direction
A contract note is the legal confirmation of executed trades, showing price, quantity, time and charges, and helps clients verify transactions and detect unauthorised trades.
A client asks the broker's dealer to trade on his behalf without specific instructions each time. The dealer should:
Trade only with valid written authorisation
Trade freely, because the client trusts him
Use the client's account to trade for other clients too
Refuse to send any trade confirmation to the client
Discretionary trading without proper written authorisation is unauthorised trading. Even with authorisation, every trade must be reported to the client and limited to that client's account.
Which practice best demonstrates fair treatment of a retail derivatives client?
Highlighting only past winning trades of other clients
Encouraging the client to borrow money to increase position size
Avoiding discussion of losses so as not to discourage him
Explaining margin calls and that losses can exceed capital

Fair dealing requires balanced disclosure of risks, including margin calls and losses beyond the initial deposit. Cherry-picked successes and encouraging borrowing for speculation are poor sales practices.
A stock broker learns that a client's position will receive a large order from the broker's institutional client and trades ahead of it for its own account. This is called:
Hedging
Front running
Arbitrage
Rebalancing
Trading ahead of a known pending client order to benefit from the expected price impact is front running, a prohibited practice. Hedging and arbitrage are legitimate strategies.
SEBI's investor charter for stock brokers primarily aims to:
Fix the brokerage that every broker must charge
Guarantee profits on all trades placed through a broker
Inform investors of their rights and redressal options
List the stocks that investors are forbidden to buy
The investor charter sets out the vision, services, rights, responsibilities and grievance redressal steps for investors dealing with brokers. It does not fix brokerage or guarantee returns.

Introduction to Capital Market.overview: This chapter sets the context for merchant banking by describing the Indian capital market: primary and secondary markets, types of securities, market participants and intermediaries, and the regulators and laws that govern them. Learn the roles of SEBI, stock exchanges, depositories, clearing corporations, registrars and bankers to an issue, and the different ways companies raise capital such as IPOs, FPOs, rights issues, QIPs and private placements. Expect straightforward questions on terms, roles and the flow of funds between issuers and investors.
questions: Which method allows a listed company to raise capital by issuing shares only to qualified institutional buyers, without a full public offer?
Rights issue to all existing shareholders
Follow-on public offer through book building
Qualified Institutions Placement
Bonus issue out of free reserves

A QIP lets a listed company place equity or convertible securities with QIBs quickly, with lighter documentation than a public issue. A rights issue goes to existing holders and a bonus issue raises no fresh money.
A company issues new shares to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings, at a price usually below market. This is a:
Rights issue
Preferential allotment to a strategic investor
Initial public offer on the main board
Offer for sale by promoters

A rights issue offers shares to existing shareholders pro rata, often at a discount, and the rights can usually be renounced. A preferential allotment goes to selected persons, and an offer for sale involves existing shares.
Which intermediary maintains the register of security holders and processes applications and allotment on behalf of an issuer?
Credit rating agency for the issuer's debt
Registrar to an issue and share transfer agent
Custodian of a foreign portfolio investor
Debenture trustee for secured bonds

The registrar (RTA) handles applications, finalises the basis of allotment with the exchange, credits securities and maintains holder records. Rating agencies rate debt, custodians hold assets for clients, and debenture trustees protect debenture holders.
A company's shares change hands between two investors on a stock exchange. What does the company receive from this trade?
The full sale value of the shares
The difference between issue price and sale price
A fee equal to the stamp duty paid
Nothing, as the trade is between investors
Secondary market trades transfer existing shares between investors; the issuer receives no money. Companies raise funds only when they issue securities in the primary market.
The main purpose of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 is to:
Regulate the issue of bank notes and coins by the government
Prevent undesirable transactions in securities
Govern the incorporation and winding up of companies
Regulate insurance and pension products sold to the public

The SCRA regulates recognition of stock exchanges, contracts in securities and listing, to prevent undesirable transactions. Currency issue is under the RBI Act, company formation under the Companies Act, and insurance under the Insurance Act.
Which of the following is a debt instrument commonly issued by companies to raise long-term funds?
Equity shares with voting rights
Sweat equity shares
Units of an equity mutual fund
Non-convertible debentures

Non-convertible debentures are debt securities that pay interest and are repaid at maturity. Equity and sweat equity shares represent ownership, and mutual fund units are issued by funds, not companies borrowing money.
Why is a depository important for a public issue in India?
It decides the price band for the issue
It underwrites the unsubscribed portion of the issue
Allotted shares are credited in demat form
It grants SEBI's approval to the offer document

Securities in public issues must be issued in dematerialised form, so depositories (NSDL and CDSL), through participants, credit allotted shares to investors. Pricing is with the issuer and lead manager, and SEBI issues observations.
A company listed on the main board makes a further public issue of fresh shares. This is called a:
Follow-on public offer
Initial public offer
Qualified institutions placement to QIBs only
Buyback of securities
An FPO is a public issue by a company that is already listed. An IPO is the first public offer by an unlisted company, a QIP is restricted to QIBs, and a buyback returns money to shareholders.

Introduction to Merchant Banking.overview: This chapter explains what merchant banking is, how it evolved in India and the range of services merchant bankers provide, including issue management, underwriting, corporate advisory, project counselling, loan syndication and takeover advisory. It introduces the SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations, 1992 and the distinction between activities that require registration and those that do not. Revise the core functions of a lead manager, the role of merchant bankers in protecting investors through due diligence, and how they coordinate other issue intermediaries.
questions: Which activity of a merchant banker involves arranging finance for a large project from a group of lenders?
Portfolio management for retail clients
Loan syndication
Market making in SME shares
Credit rating of the project's bonds

Loan syndication means bringing together several banks or institutions to jointly lend to a project. Portfolio management and credit rating are separate regulated activities, and market making is a trading function in SME issues.
In a public issue with several lead managers, how is the work usually divided?
Only one lead manager is allowed to sign the due diligence certificate
SEBI assigns each lead manager to a different class of investors
The registrar decides which lead manager handles which task
Their responsibilities are allocated and disclosed

When more than one lead manager is appointed, the inter se allocation of responsibilities is set out and disclosed in the offer document, so accountability for each activity is clear. All lead managers remain responsible for due diligence.
A merchant banker advising a company on how to restructure its capital and raise funds is performing:
Corporate advisory services
Depository participant services
Stock broking services
Registrar and transfer agent services

Advising on capital structure, fund-raising options and restructuring is corporate advisory, a traditional merchant banking service. Depository, broking and RTA services are separate intermediary functions with their own registrations.
Which of the following is the best description of the 'issue manager' role?
Holding the issue proceeds in an escrow account for the issuer
Crediting allotted shares to investors' demat accounts
Planning the issue and filing documents with SEBI
Matching buy and sell orders on the exchange after listing

The issue manager (lead manager) plans the issue, conducts due diligence, prepares the offer document, files it with SEBI and coordinates other intermediaries. Bankers hold funds, depositories credit shares and exchanges match trades.
A merchant banker underwrites ₹10 crore of a public issue. If the issue is undersubscribed and investors take up only ₹6 crore of that portion, the merchant banker must:
Return the ₹6 crore to the investors
Ask SEBI to cancel the issue immediately
Pay a penalty of ₹4 crore to the stock exchange
Take up or procure the balance ₹4 crore

Underwriting is a commitment to take up the shortfall. The underwriter must subscribe to, or arrange subscribers for, the unsubscribed ₹4 crore of its commitment. The issue is not automatically cancelled.
Why is a merchant banker described as a 'gatekeeper' of the primary market?
Its due diligence screens issues before they reach investors
It decides which investors may trade in the secondary market
It fixes the listing fee charged by stock exchanges
It guarantees a minimum listing-day gain for investors

Merchant bankers verify disclosures and compliance before an issue is launched, acting as a first line of protection for investors. They do not control secondary trading, set exchange fees or guarantee returns.
Which of the following services would a merchant banker typically NOT provide?
Managing public issues of securities
Advising on mergers and takeovers
Accepting public deposits like a commercial bank
Underwriting issues of securities
Accepting deposits from the public is a banking activity regulated by the RBI. Issue management, M&A advisory and underwriting are core merchant banking activities under SEBI regulations.
In project counselling, a merchant banker mainly helps a client with:
Collecting application forms from investors at bank branches
Assessing project viability and preparing a financing plan
Holding the client's shares in a depository account
Clearing and settling the client's stock trades

Project counselling covers feasibility studies, cost estimates, means of finance and preparing project reports for lenders. The other options are functions of bankers, depositories and clearing corporations.

Registration, Code of Conduct & Obligati.overview: This chapter covers how a merchant banker gets registered with SEBI, the eligibility and capital adequacy requirements, the fit and proper person criteria, the code of conduct, general obligations and responsibilities, record keeping, appointment of a compliance officer and SEBI's powers of inspection and action. Requirements are amended from time to time, so focus on principles: who may register, what conduct is expected, which conflicts are prohibited and what happens on breach. Expect scenario questions on ethics and conflicts of interest.
questions: A merchant banker wants to lead manage an issue in which it holds a significant stake through an associate. Which concern does this mainly raise?
Insufficient number of employees for the issue
A conflict of interest
Failure to pay the stamp duty on the issue
Breach of minimum public shareholding norms

SEBI rules restrict a merchant banker from lead managing an issue of an associated entity because its objectivity in due diligence is compromised. The concern is conflict of interest, not staffing or public shareholding.
Which is an essential condition for SEBI to grant a certificate of registration to a merchant banker?
It meets the 'fit and proper person' criteria
The applicant has already completed at least ten public issues
The applicant is listed on a recognised stock exchange
The applicant is owned by a public sector bank

SEBI assesses integrity, reputation, competence and financial soundness under the fit and proper criteria. Prior issue experience, listing or public sector ownership are not preconditions for registration.
A merchant banker's employee prepares marketing material claiming the IPO 'will surely list at a 50% premium'. Under the code of conduct this is:
Permitted if the grey market premium supports it
Permitted if the issuer approves the statement
Not permitted, as it is a misleading assurance of returns
Permitted for issues reserved for retail investors
The code of conduct prohibits misleading statements and assurances of returns or listing gains. Grey market indications or issuer approval do not make such promises acceptable.
For how long must a merchant banker generally preserve books of account, records and documents?
Only until the issue gets listed
Only for the current financial year
Until the next SEBI inspection is completed
For the minimum period set by SEBI regulations

Merchant bankers must maintain prescribed books and records and preserve them for the minimum period laid down in the regulations, so SEBI can inspect past issues. Discarding records after listing or one year would breach this.
SEBI wants to examine whether a merchant banker's records comply with the regulations. Which power can it use?
Revocation of the company's incorporation certificate
Freezing of the merchant banker's employees' salaries
Inspection of the merchant banker's books and records
Taking over the management of the issuer company

SEBI can inspect a merchant banker's books, records and documents and follow up with directions or penalties. Company incorporation is under the Registrar of Companies, and SEBI does not take over issuer management in such cases.
A merchant banker is asked by a client to suppress adverse information from an offer document. What should it do?
Refuse, because full and true disclosure is its obligation
Agree, provided the client pays a higher fee
Agree, but mention the matter only to SEBI orally
Agree if the information is less than one year old
Merchant bankers must ensure the offer document contains all material information and must not suppress facts. Fee levels or informal disclosure to SEBI cannot justify misleading investors.
Which of the following is a duty of the compliance officer of a merchant banker?
Deciding the price band of every issue managed by the firm
Approving the issuer's annual financial statements
Allotting shares to investors in every public issue
Monitoring compliance and reporting lapses to SEBI
The compliance officer monitors adherence to SEBI rules, circulars and regulations and must report any non-compliance observed to SEBI. Pricing, audit approval and allotment are handled by others.
A merchant banker receives an order from SEBI imposing a penalty. If aggrieved, it may appeal to:
The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
The Securities Appellate Tribunal
The Insurance Ombudsman
The Reserve Bank of India

Appeals against SEBI orders lie with the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT), and further to the Supreme Court. Consumer forums, the Insurance Ombudsman and RBI do not hear appeals against SEBI orders.

Issue Management – Important Terms.overview: This chapter covers the vocabulary of public issues under the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations: book building, fixed price issue, price band, floor price, cap price, cut-off price, anchor investors, QIBs, non-institutional and retail investors, red herring prospectus, abridged prospectus, offer for sale, fresh issue, green shoe option, ASBA, UPI mandate, basis of allotment and listing. When revising, be precise about who each investor category includes, how prices are discovered in book building and what each document contains.
questions: In a book-built issue, the price band is announced and the floor price is ₹400. What is the maximum cap price permitted?
The cap of the price band cannot exceed 120% of the floor price, so the maximum cap = 1.2 × ₹400 = ₹480. ₹500 would be 125% of the floor and is not permitted.
Which document contains the final issue price and number of securities after book building is completed?
Prospectus filed with the Registrar of Companies
Draft red herring prospectus
Abridged prospectus attached to the bid form
Price band advertisement

After bids close, the final price and issue size are included in the prospectus filed with the RoC. The DRHP and RHP do not contain the final price, and the price band advertisement only states the range.
Bidders applying for more than ₹2 lakh in a public issue who are not QIBs fall under the category of:
Retail individual investors
Anchor investors
Qualified institutional buyers
Non-institutional investors
Applicants who are not QIBs and bid above ₹2 lakh are non-institutional investors (NIIs). Retail individual investors bid up to ₹2 lakh, while anchors and QIBs are institutional categories.
Which of the following is an example of a qualified institutional buyer (QIB) under ICDR?
A resident individual with a large portfolio
A Hindu Undivided Family investing ₹5 lakh
A SEBI-registered mutual fund
A partnership firm dealing in textiles

QIBs include mutual funds, banks, insurers, pension funds, FPIs (other than certain categories) and similar institutions. Individuals, HUFs and ordinary partnership firms are not QIBs, regardless of investment size.
In the 'basis of allotment' for an oversubscribed retail portion of a main-board IPO, the general principle is to:
Allot shares only to the largest retail applicants first
Allot shares in proportion to each applicant's annual income
Give the minimum bid lot to as many applicants as possible
Allot shares only to applicants who bid above the cut-off
ICDR requires that, where possible, each retail applicant gets at least the minimum bid lot, with draw of lots if needed. Size priority or income has no role, and cut-off bids are valid retail bids.
The minimum bid lot in a main-board IPO is designed so that the minimum application value falls:
Above ₹2 lakh, to exclude retail investors
Within a band prescribed by SEBI
At exactly ₹1 lakh for every issue
At whatever value the anchor investors decide

SEBI prescribes a band for the minimum application size so that small investors can participate. The issuer and lead manager set the lot within that band; it is not fixed at a single value or decided by anchors.
An 'abridged prospectus' is:
A summary of salient features sent with the bid form
A prospectus filed only with the stock exchange and not with SEBI
A document issued only for debt securities
The final prospectus after deletion of risk factors
The abridged prospectus summarises key information and must accompany application forms so investors see the essentials. Risk factors cannot be dropped; it complements the full offer document.
In a book-built issue, what does 'cut-off price' mean for a retail bidder?
Bidding at the floor price only
Bidding at a price below the floor price
Withdrawing the bid if the price is above the floor
Accepting the final price discovered within the band
A cut-off bid means the investor accepts the final issue price determined within the band. Such bidders block funds at the cap price so that their bid remains valid whatever the final price.

Issue Management – Process & Underwritin.overview: This chapter describes the end-to-end process of a public issue under ICDR: appointment of intermediaries, eligibility norms, due diligence, filing the draft offer document, SEBI observations, roadshows, price band announcement, bidding through ASBA and UPI, allocation among investor categories, basis of allotment, refunds and listing. It also covers underwriting, minimum subscription and promoter contribution. Revise the sequence of steps, the reservation percentages under regulation 6(1) and 6(2), and the rules on promoter contribution and lock-in, using numerical examples.
questions: A company's post-issue paid-up equity capital will be ₹50 crore. What is the minimum promoter contribution required in its IPO under ICDR?
₹5 crore
₹12.5 crore
₹25 crore
₹10 crore
Promoters must contribute at least 20% of the post-issue capital: 20% × ₹50 crore = ₹10 crore. ₹12.5 crore would be 25%, which reflects confusion with the minimum public shareholding norm.
In a book-built IPO under regulation 6(1) of ICDR, what is the minimum share of the issue to be allocated to retail individual investors?
Under regulation 6(1), not less than 35% goes to retail investors, not less than 15% to non-institutional investors and not more than 50% to QIBs. 10% retail applies to issuers under regulation 6(2).
Which step must occur before the red herring prospectus is filed with the Registrar of Companies?
Listing of the shares on the stock exchange
Finalisation of the basis of allotment
Receipt of SEBI's observations on the draft offer document
Credit of shares to the investors' demat accounts
The DRHP is filed with SEBI and the issue proceeds only after SEBI's observations are incorporated. Basis of allotment, credit of shares and listing all happen after the issue closes.
An issuer revises the price band during the bidding period. What must it do as a result?
Extend the bidding period by some working days
Cancel all bids already received and invite fresh bids
Refile the draft offer document with SEBI
Reduce the issue size by half

On revision of the price band, the bid period must be extended by at least three working days, subject to the overall maximum, with wide publicity. Existing bids are not cancelled and refiling is not required.
Under UPI-based ASBA, what happens to a retail investor's money when he bids?
The amount is blocked in his bank account until allotment is finalised
The amount is debited and paid to the issuer immediately
The amount is transferred to the lead manager's own account
Nothing happens until shares are listed

Under ASBA, funds stay in the investor's account but are blocked through a UPI mandate. On allotment, only the amount for allotted shares is debited and the rest unblocked; there is no transfer to the lead manager.
In a firm underwriting arrangement, the underwriter:
Subscribes only if the issue is fully subscribed by the public
Has no obligation if the issue fails
Is paid only if the shares list at a premium
Commits to take a fixed number of shares in any case

In firm underwriting, the underwriter commits to take up a specified number of securities irrespective of subscription by the public, in addition to any devolvement obligation. Its commission does not depend on listing gains.
A company does not satisfy the track record conditions under regulation 6(1) and comes with an IPO under regulation 6(2). Which allocation rule applies?
At least 75% of the net offer must be allotted to retail investors
At least 75% of the net offer must be allotted to QIBs
At most 25% of the net offer can be allotted to QIBs
The entire issue must be allotted to anchor investors

Issuers coming under regulation 6(2) must allot at least 75% of the net offer to QIBs, with not more than 15% to NIIs and not more than 10% to retail investors, since such companies carry higher risk.
Which is the correct order of these IPO steps?
Bidding, filing of DRHP, allotment, SEBI observations, filing of RHP
Filing of RHP, bidding, filing of DRHP, SEBI observations, allotment
Filing of DRHP, SEBI observations, filing of RHP, bidding, allotment
SEBI observations, filing of DRHP, allotment, bidding, filing of RHP
The draft is filed with SEBI first, SEBI gives observations, the RHP is filed with the RoC, bidding opens, and allotment follows issue closure. Bidding cannot precede the offer document.

Issue Management – Obligations & Due Dil.overview: This chapter covers the responsibilities of the lead manager before, during and after a public issue: due diligence on the issuer, promoters and disclosures, the due diligence certificates, coordination with the monitoring agency, advertisement norms, post-issue monitoring, handling of investor grievances, refunds and reporting to SEBI. Key ideas are that the lead manager must verify, not just compile, information; must ensure advertisements are fair; and continues to be responsible after the issue closes. Expect scenario questions on red flags discovered during due diligence.
questions: While reviewing a draft offer document, the lead manager finds that a promoter director has been declared a wilful defaulter. What is the correct approach?
Ignore it, since only the company's own record matters
Disclose it only after listing to avoid affecting demand
Remove the director's name from the offer document
Treat it as material, as such issuers face ICDR curbs

ICDR restricts issuers whose promoters or directors are wilful defaulters or fugitive economic offenders from making public issues. The lead manager must treat this as material; hiding it or deferring disclosure would breach due diligence obligations.
Issue advertisements prepared by the issuer and lead manager must:
Highlight expected listing gains to attract investors
Mention only the positive aspects of the issuer
Be truthful, fair and consistent with the offer document
Avoid any reference to risk factors

ICDR advertisement norms require advertisements to be fair, not misleading, and consistent with the offer document; they cannot promise returns or omit material risks. Selective positive messaging would mislead investors.
After the issue, investors complain of delays in unblocking funds for unallotted bids. Who is primarily responsible for coordinating the redress?
The stock exchange's listing department alone
The lead manager, with the registrar and SCSBs
The credit rating agency that rated the issuer
SEBI's chairman personally

The lead manager continues to coordinate post-issue activities, including refunds, unblocking and grievance redress, with the registrar and SCSBs. Rating agencies have no role, and SEBI oversees rather than handles each complaint.
A monitoring agency appointed for an IPO reports that issue proceeds are being used for purposes not stated in the offer document. This deviation:
Must be disclosed, and a change in objects needs shareholder approval
Can be ignored if the amount is below 50% of the issue
Is permitted without any approval within three years
Must be reported only to the company's auditors

Proceeds must be used for stated objects. Any variation requires shareholders' approval by special resolution and appropriate disclosures, with exit options where applicable. Deviations cannot simply be ignored.
In due diligence, which approach reflects a merchant banker's proper standard?
Independently verifying key claims made by management
Copying management's statements into the offer document without checks
Relying only on the previous year's newspaper reports
Verifying information only if SEBI specifically asks for it

Due diligence requires reasonable independent verification through documents, site visits, legal and financial checks and confirmations. Mere reproduction of management claims does not meet the standard expected of a lead manager.
Which of the following must be disclosed as a risk factor if material?
The name of the advertising agency for the issue
The colour scheme of the company's logo
The personal hobbies of the company's directors
Pending litigation that could hurt operations
Material litigation, regulatory actions and business risks must be disclosed so investors can assess the issue. Trivial details such as advertising agencies or logos are not risk factors.
When must a lead manager file a due diligence certificate with SEBI in an IPO?
Only after the shares have listed
Only if SEBI raises a query on the issue
With the draft offer document and at later stages
Only when the issue is undersubscribed

Due diligence certificates are filed with the draft offer document and at specified later stages, such as filing with the RoC, confirming continued accuracy. They are not optional or triggered only by queries.
A lead manager learns of a material adverse development about the issuer after the RHP is filed but before bidding closes. It should:
Ignore it, since the RHP has already been filed
Ensure it is disclosed before the issue closes
Disclose it only in the next annual report
Inform only anchor investors privately

The lead manager must ensure investors receive updated material information, typically through an addendum or public notice, before they commit. Selective disclosure to anchors would be unfair and violate disclosure norms.

Mergers, Acquisitions & Takeovers.overview: This chapter covers corporate restructuring and takeovers: types of mergers, amalgamations and demergers, schemes of arrangement under the Companies Act, valuation in M&A, and the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011. Key SAST concepts are triggers for open offers, creeping acquisitions, offer size, offer price, disclosures, voluntary and competing offers, withdrawal and the role of the manager to the open offer. Revise thresholds and timelines carefully and practise simple calculations on offer size and creeping acquisition.
questions: A listed company has 10 crore shares. An acquirer crosses the 25% threshold and must make a mandatory open offer for the minimum size. How many shares must the offer cover?
2.5 crore shares
1.0 crore shares
5.1 crore shares
2.6 crore shares
The minimum open offer size is 26% of the total shares: 26% × 10 crore = 2.6 crore shares. 2.5 crore reflects the trigger level, not the offer size.
An acquirer holds 40% of a listed company. Under the creeping acquisition route, what is the maximum holding it can reach by acquisitions in one financial year without an open offer?
An acquirer holding 25% or more but below the maximum permissible non-public shareholding may acquire up to 5% more in a financial year without an open offer: 40% + 5% = 45%.
A merger in which two companies in the same industry and at the same stage of production combine is a:
Vertical merger
Horizontal merger
Conglomerate merger
Reverse merger
A horizontal merger joins competitors in the same line of business. A vertical merger joins firms at different stages of the supply chain, and a conglomerate merger joins unrelated businesses.
An acquirer who already holds 30% of a target makes an open offer voluntarily to consolidate control. What is the minimum size of such a voluntary offer?
26% of the total shares
5% of the total shares
10% of the total shares
51% of the total shares

A voluntary open offer by an acquirer holding 25% or more must be for at least 10% of the total shares, without exceeding the maximum permissible non-public shareholding. The 26% minimum applies to mandatory offers.
Which of the following can trigger an open offer obligation under SAST even without crossing a shareholding threshold?
Purchase of 1% of shares by a mutual fund
Receipt of a bonus issue by an existing holder
Grant of ESOPs to employees
Acquisition of control over the target company

SAST requires an open offer when an acquirer acquires control, directly or indirectly, regardless of the percentage acquired. Small purchases, bonus issues and ESOP grants do not by themselves trigger an open offer.
A company transfers one of its divisions to a new company, whose shares are issued to the original company's shareholders. This is a:
Horizontal merger
Buyback of shares
Demerger
Rights issue
In a demerger, an undertaking is transferred to a resulting company, which issues shares to the demerged company's shareholders. It splits a business rather than combining two businesses.
After an acquirer announces an open offer, another person announces a competing offer for the same target within the permitted time. What is the general effect?
The first offer is automatically cancelled
Shareholders may choose either offer
SEBI decides which offer shareholders must accept
The target company must reject both offers
SAST allows competing offers within a specified period. Both offers proceed on a common schedule, acquirers may revise their offers, and shareholders decide which to tender into.
Under SAST, the offer price in a mandatory open offer is broadly set as:
The highest of several benchmark prices specified in the regulations
Any price the acquirer chooses, without reference to the market
The face value of the shares
The lowest price at which the stock traded in the last week

The offer price must be at least the highest of benchmarks such as the negotiated price, the highest price paid by the acquirer in a look-back period and the volume-weighted average market price, protecting public shareholders.

Disinvestment & Buyback.overview: This chapter covers two ways in which ownership changes without a regular public issue. Disinvestment is the government's sale of its stake in public sector enterprises through methods such as IPOs, offer for sale through stock exchanges, strategic sale and ETFs, managed by DIPAM. Buyback is a company repurchasing its own shares under the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI (Buy-back of Securities) Regulations, through permitted routes such as tender offer. Revise sources and limits of buyback, approvals needed, debt-equity conditions, gaps between buybacks and how shares bought back are treated.
questions: A company's paid-up capital is ₹200 crore and its free reserves are ₹800 crore. What is the maximum buyback it can make with only board approval?
₹250 crore
₹200 crore
₹100 crore
₹80 crore
With board approval alone, a buyback is limited to 10% of paid-up capital plus free reserves: 10% × (₹200 + ₹800) crore = ₹100 crore. A special resolution allows up to 25%, which would be ₹250 crore.
What happens to shares bought back by a company?
They are held as treasury shares and resold later
They are transferred to the promoters free of cost
They are given to employees as bonus shares
They are extinguished within the prescribed time
Shares bought back must be extinguished within the time prescribed; Indian law does not allow companies to hold them as treasury stock for resale. They cannot be passed on to promoters or employees.
In which method of disinvestment does the government sell a significant stake along with management control to a buyer?
Strategic sale
Offer for sale through stock exchange
Exchange traded fund route
Minority stake sale in an IPO
A strategic sale transfers a substantial stake and management control to a strategic buyer. OFS, ETFs and minority IPO sales reduce the government's holding without handing over control.
A company can fund a buyback of its equity shares out of:
Proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of equity shares
Free reserves, securities premium or other-kind issue proceeds
Borrowed funds that take its debt to five times equity
Money received as share application money pending allotment

The Companies Act permits buyback out of free reserves, securities premium or proceeds of any shares or specified securities other than those of the same kind. Using proceeds of the same kind of shares is prohibited.
Under the current tax rules effective from October 2024, money received by a resident shareholder on a buyback of shares is:
Fully exempt in the hands of the shareholder
Treated as a dividend and taxed in the shareholder's hands
Taxed only in the company's hands at a flat rate
Taxed as long-term capital gain at 10%

From 1 October 2024, buyback proceeds are treated as deemed dividend taxable in the shareholder's hands, with the cost of shares treated as a capital loss. Earlier, the company paid buyback tax and holders were exempt.
The government sells a portion of its holding in a listed PSU through the stock exchange's dedicated window for promoters. This is called:
Qualified institutions placement
Rights issue
Offer for sale through the exchange
Preferential allotment

The OFS mechanism lets promoters, including the government, sell shares of listed companies through a separate exchange window. QIPs, rights issues and preferential allotments involve the company issuing fresh shares.
Which of the following is a reason a company may undertake a buyback?
To return surplus cash to shareholders
To increase the number of shares outstanding
To raise fresh capital for expansion
To reduce its free reserves to zero by law
Buybacks return excess cash, reduce share count and can raise EPS and return on equity. They reduce, not increase, shares outstanding and do not raise new capital.
Units of the CPSE ETF and the Bharat 22 ETF, sold to investors by the government, represent which disinvestment method?
Strategic sale with transfer of control
Buyback of shares by each CPSE
Rights issue by the government
Exchange traded fund route

Through the ETF route, the government sells its holdings in a basket of CPSEs to an ETF, whose units investors buy. This divests stakes across many companies without transferring control, unlike a strategic sale.

Investment Advisory & Financial Planning.overview: This chapter introduces investment advisory and financial planning: the difference between advice and product distribution, the steps of the financial planning process, client life-cycle stages, goal setting and the importance of risk profiling and suitability. It also covers the adviser's role as a fiduciary who puts the client's interest first. When revising, learn the sequence of planning steps, how goals are prioritised and quantified, and why understanding the client's full financial situation must come before any product recommendation.
questions: A client says his goal is 'to be rich some day'. What should the adviser do first to make this goal usable in a plan?
Recommend a small-cap equity fund straight away
Help him define it in amount and time terms
Ignore it and focus only on his tax-saving needs for the current year
Ask him to choose a product from a list of popular schemes
A planning goal must be specific, measurable and time-bound, so the adviser converts a vague wish into a target amount and date. Only then can the required savings and asset allocation be worked out.
Which statement best distinguishes an investment adviser from a mutual fund distributor?
The adviser can sell any product and earn commission from each fund house
The distributor must charge a fixed fee directly to the client
The adviser is paid by the client for advice
Both are paid in the same way and have identical obligations

A SEBI-registered investment adviser is remunerated only by the client and must act in the client's interest. A distributor is paid commissions by product manufacturers, which creates a different set of incentives.
A 52-year-old client with grown-up children and a paid-off home is most likely in which life-cycle stage?
