Consolidation, nearing retirement
Early accumulation, just starting a career
Distribution, already drawing a pension for many years
Dependence on parents for financial support
In the consolidation stage, income is near its peak, major liabilities are largely settled and the focus shifts to building and protecting the retirement corpus. Distribution begins after retirement.
Why is a periodic review an essential step of the financial planning process?
SEBI requires advisers to change the portfolio every month
Reviews allow the adviser to earn additional commissions
A plan once made can never be modified, so reviews only confirm it
Client circumstances and markets change over time
Income, goals, family situation, tax laws and market conditions change, so a plan must be monitored and updated. Reviews are not about churning the portfolio or earning commissions.
Two clients have the same income and age. One is anxious about any fall in value; the other is comfortable with volatility. This difference relates mainly to their:
Risk capacity
Investment horizon
Liquidity needs
Risk tolerance
Risk tolerance is the psychological willingness to accept volatility. Risk capacity is the financial ability to bear losses, which here appears similar because income and age are the same.
An adviser recommends a product mainly because it pays her a higher fee from the issuer, though a cheaper suitable option exists. This breaches the principle of:
Acting in the client's best interest
Diversification across asset classes
Rupee cost averaging
Tax efficiency of investment products
A fiduciary must place the client's interest ahead of her own. Choosing a product for personal gain when a better suitable option exists is a conflict of interest and a breach of fiduciary duty.
Which piece of information is most important to collect before preparing a client's asset allocation?
The brand of car he plans to buy next year
His goals, time horizon and risk profile
The names of funds his friends have bought recently
His preferred stock exchange for trading shares
Asset allocation depends on what the money is for, when it is needed and how much risk the client can and will take. Peer choices and trivial preferences do not drive allocation.
A client has three goals: emergency fund, child's education in 12 years and a foreign holiday next year. Which is generally prioritised first?
The foreign holiday next year
The child's education in 12 years
The emergency fund
All goals should be funded equally from the start

An emergency fund protects all other goals from being derailed by sudden expenses or income loss, so it is usually the first priority. Essential long-term goals come next, and discretionary goals after that.

Time Value of Money.overview: This chapter covers the time value of money: compounding and discounting, future and present value of lump sums and annuities, ordinary annuity versus annuity due, effective annual rates, real versus nominal returns, loan EMIs and rules of thumb such as the rule of 72. These tools underpin goal planning and loan analysis. When revising, practise calculations with a financial calculator or spreadsheet, be careful about compounding frequency and payment timing, and interpret results in client terms.
questions: Using the rule of 72, roughly how many years will an investment take to double at 9% per annum?
9 years
6 years
12 years
8 years
The rule of 72 estimates doubling time as 72 ÷ interest rate = 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years. The exact figure at 9% annual compounding is about 8.04 years, so the approximation is close.
A deposit earns 10% per annum while inflation is 6%. What is the real rate of return, using the exact formula?
Exactly 4.00%
About 16.6%
About 3.77%
About 1.67%
Real return = (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1 = 1.10 ÷ 1.06 − 1 ≈ 3.77%. Simply subtracting 6% from 10% gives 4%, which slightly overstates the real return.
A home loan of ₹20 lakh is taken at 9% per annum for 15 years with monthly EMIs. The EMI is closest to:
EMI = P × r × (1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1) with r = 0.75% and n = 180, giving about ₹20,285. ₹11,111 ignores interest and ₹15,000 is only the first month's interest.
An investment grew from ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh in 6 years. What is its compound annual growth rate?
About 12.2%
About 16.7%
About 10.0%
About 14.5%
CAGR = (2 ÷ 1)^(1/6) − 1 ≈ 12.25%. 16.7% is the simple average (100% ÷ 6), which ignores compounding and overstates the annual growth rate.
What is the present value of ₹50,000 received at the end of each year for 10 years, discounted at 8% per annum?
PV of an ordinary annuity = 50,000 × (1 − 1.08^−10) ÷ 0.08 ≈ ₹3,35,504. ₹3,62,344 is the annuity-due value with payments at the start of each year, and ₹5,00,000 ignores discounting.
₹5 lakh is invested for 3 years at 8% per annum compounded quarterly. Its maturity value is closest to:
Quarterly rate 2% for 12 quarters: 5,00,000 × 1.02^12 ≈ ₹6,34,121. Annual compounding gives ₹6,29,856 and simple interest gives ₹6,20,000, both lower because interest compounds less often.
Compared with an ordinary annuity of the same amount, rate and term, the future value of an annuity due is:
Lower, because payments are made later
Exactly the same in all cases
Higher only when the interest rate is negative
Higher, as each payment earns one extra period
An annuity due has payments at the start of each period, so every payment compounds for one more period. Its value equals the ordinary annuity value multiplied by (1 + r).
If the discount rate used to value a future goal increases, the present value of that goal will:
Fall
Rise
Stay the same
Double
Present value = future value ÷ (1 + r)^n. A higher discount rate increases the denominator, so the present value falls. This is why the assumed return strongly affects required savings.

Client Financial Position & Debt Managem.overview: This chapter teaches how to assess a client's financial position using the personal balance sheet (net worth statement) and cash flow statement, and key ratios such as savings ratio, liquidity ratio, solvency ratio and debt-to-income. It also covers emergency funds, good versus bad debt, loan prioritisation, prepayment decisions and credit scores. When revising, practise computing these ratios from data and recommending sensible actions, such as repaying expensive debt first or building a liquid buffer.
questions: A family's essential monthly expenses are ₹60,000. If the adviser recommends an emergency fund of six months' expenses, how much should it be?
Emergency fund = monthly essential expenses × months of cover = 60,000 × 6 = ₹3,60,000. ₹7,20,000 would be twelve months and ₹1,80,000 only three months.
A client's monthly take-home income is ₹1,50,000 and her monthly expenses including EMIs are ₹1,05,000. What is her savings ratio?
Savings = 1,50,000 − 1,05,000 = ₹45,000. Savings ratio = 45,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = 30%. 70% is the share of income spent, not saved.
A client has total assets of ₹1 crore and total liabilities of ₹40 lakh. What is the solvency ratio (net worth ÷ total assets)?
Net worth = ₹1 crore − ₹40 lakh = ₹60 lakh. Solvency ratio = 60 lakh ÷ 1 crore = 60%. 40% is the liabilities-to-assets ratio, the complement of solvency.
Which of the following is generally considered 'good debt'?
A credit card balance used to fund a holiday
A personal loan taken to buy the latest smartphone
An education loan for a skill that raises income
A loan taken to speculate in futures and options
Good debt finances assets or capabilities that are likely to grow in value or raise earning power. Consumption debt and borrowing to speculate do not create such value and often carry high cost.
A client has ₹2 lakh surplus. She has a car loan at 9%, a personal loan at 15% and a home loan at 8.5% with tax benefits. Which should she prepay first?
The home loan at 8.5%
The car loan at 9%
The personal loan at 15%
Split the money equally across all three loans
Prepaying the highest-cost debt gives the greatest guaranteed saving. The personal loan at 15% is costliest; the home loan is cheapest after tax benefits, so it should be prepaid last.
A personal cash flow statement differs from a net worth statement because it shows:
Assets and liabilities at a point in time
Inflows and outflows over a period
Only the market value of investments held
Only the tax payable by the client
A cash flow statement records income and expenses over a period, showing the surplus available. The net worth statement is a snapshot of assets minus liabilities on a given date.
A client's liquid assets are ₹2,40,000 and monthly expenses are ₹80,000. His liquidity ratio (in months of expenses) is:
3 months
2 months
6 months
0.33 months
Liquidity ratio = liquid assets ÷ monthly expenses = 2,40,000 ÷ 80,000 = 3 months. It shows how long the client can meet expenses from liquid funds if income stops.
Which action is most likely to improve a client's credit score over time?
Applying for several new loans in the same month
Using the full credit card limit every month
Closing the oldest credit card and missing a payment
Paying all EMIs and card dues on time
Timely repayment is the biggest factor in credit scores. Multiple applications, high credit utilisation and missed payments all lower the score.

Indian Financial Markets.overview: This chapter gives an overview of the Indian financial system: money markets and capital markets, their instruments, participants and regulators. Money market instruments include treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, call money and repo, while capital markets cover equity, bonds and related products. Regulators include the RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA. Focus on which regulator oversees which market or product, the typical tenor and issuer of each instrument, and the role of financial intermediaries in channelling savings into investment.
questions: Which instrument is issued by banks to raise short-term funds and is a money market instrument?
Commercial paper
Certificate of deposit
Treasury bill
Equity share

Certificates of deposit are issued by banks and certain financial institutions. Commercial paper is issued by companies, treasury bills by the government through the RBI, and equity shares are capital market instruments.
Treasury bills in India are currently issued with which maturities?
30, 60 and 90 days
1, 3 and 5 years
7, 14 and 28 days
91, 182 and 364 days
The Government of India issues treasury bills of 91, 182 and 364 days through RBI auctions. They are issued at a discount and redeemed at face value.
Which regulator oversees the National Pension System?
IRDAI
SEBI
PFRDA
NABARD
The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority regulates NPS and pension funds. IRDAI regulates insurance, SEBI regulates securities markets and NABARD is a development bank for agriculture.
In a repo transaction, a bank:
Sells securities and agrees to buy them back later
Buys shares permanently from the RBI
Issues new equity to the public
Lends money without any collateral
In a repo, the borrower sells securities with an agreement to repurchase them at a set price, making it a collateralised loan. The difference in prices is the interest, called the repo rate.
Which of these is a function of financial intermediaries such as banks and mutual funds?
Printing currency notes for circulation
Setting the policy repo rate
Pooling savings and channelling them into investment
Passing laws on taxation of income

Intermediaries mobilise savings from many households and allocate them to borrowers and issuers, offering diversification and liquidity. Currency issue and policy rates are RBI functions; tax laws are made by Parliament.
Commercial paper is typically issued by:
The central government to fund long-term deficits
Highly rated corporates for short-term funds
Retail investors to borrow from banks
Stock exchanges to finance trading members

Commercial paper is an unsecured short-term promissory note issued by creditworthy companies and certain financial institutions to meet working capital needs. Governments use T-bills and dated securities.
Which statement about the capital market is correct?
It deals in long-term instruments like shares and bonds
It deals only in instruments maturing within one year
It is regulated mainly by IRDAI
It does not include any secondary market trading
The capital market provides long-term funds through equity and debt securities and includes both primary issues and secondary trading. Instruments under one year belong to the money market.
Since the merger of the Forward Markets Commission with SEBI in 2015, commodity derivatives exchanges are regulated by:
RBI
Ministry of Agriculture
Competition Commission of India
SEBI
The FMC was merged into SEBI in September 2015, bringing commodity derivatives under SEBI's regulation alongside securities markets. RBI regulates money and forex markets, not commodity exchanges.

Securities Market Segments.overview: This chapter describes the segments of the Indian securities market: the primary market for new issues, the secondary market for trading, and the equity cash, equity derivatives, currency, commodity and debt segments. It also covers SME platforms, government securities access for retail investors, and the roles of exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories. When revising, focus on what trades in each segment, how retail investors can access bonds and G-secs, and the basic process of an IPO and secondary trade.
questions: A small and medium enterprise wants to list with lighter eligibility norms than the main board. Where can it list?
The currency derivatives segment
The commodity derivatives segment
The negotiated dealing system of the RBI
The SME platform of a stock exchange

Exchanges run dedicated SME platforms (such as NSE Emerge and BSE SME) with separate eligibility and disclosure norms for smaller companies. Derivatives segments and NDS are for trading other instruments.
Through RBI Retail Direct, an individual investor can:
Trade equity options directly with the RBI
Buy unlisted shares of private companies
Open a gilt account and buy government securities
Invest in foreign stocks without any limit

RBI Retail Direct lets individuals open a Retail Direct Gilt account with the RBI to buy G-secs in primary auctions and trade on NDS-OM. It does not cover equity options, unlisted shares or foreign stocks.
In which segment would a trader buy USD/INR futures?
Equity cash segment
Currency derivatives segment
Debt segment
SME platform

USD/INR futures and options trade in the currency derivatives segment of recognised exchanges. The equity cash segment is for shares, the debt segment for bonds and the SME platform for small company shares.
An investor buys shares of a listed company from another investor on the exchange. This trade takes place in the:
Secondary market
Primary market
Money market
Over-the-counter forward market
Trading in already-issued securities between investors happens in the secondary market. The primary market is where issuers sell new securities to raise capital.
Which entity guarantees settlement of trades executed on a stock exchange?
The depository participant
The clearing corporation
The registrar and transfer agent
The issuing company

The clearing corporation acts as central counterparty through novation and guarantees settlement. Depository participants hold demat accounts, RTAs maintain issuer records and the issuer has no role in trade settlement.
Online bond platform providers that sell listed debt securities to retail investors are regulated by:
IRDAI
PFRDA
SEBI
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs

SEBI regulates online bond platform providers, which must be registered as stock brokers in the debt segment and offer only listed or to-be-listed debt securities. IRDAI and PFRDA regulate insurance and pensions.
Why do exchanges maintain separate trading segments for equity, derivatives, currency and debt?
To ensure that investors can trade only one product type in their life
Because each segment is owned by a different government ministry
So that prices in one segment are never linked to another
Each has its own contracts and risk rules

Different instruments need different contract specifications, margins and settlement processes, so exchanges organise them into segments. Investors can trade in several segments, and prices across segments are closely linked.
A company's first-ever offer of shares to the public, followed by listing, is called:
An initial public offer
A follow-on public offer
A rights issue
A buyback offer
An IPO is the first sale of shares to the public by an unlisted company, after which it lists on an exchange. An FPO is by a listed company, and rights issues go only to existing holders.

Equity Investment.overview: This chapter covers equity as an asset class: features of equity shares, sources of equity returns, risks, corporate actions such as bonus issues, splits, rights and dividends, and basic valuation measures like EPS, P/E, P/B and dividend yield. It also covers market-cap categories and investment styles such as growth and value. When revising, practise computing simple ratios, understand how corporate actions change share count and price, and know why equity suits long horizons.
questions: A company's net profit is ₹50 crore and it has 10 crore shares outstanding. What is its earnings per share?
EPS = net profit available to equity shareholders ÷ number of shares = 50 crore ÷ 10 crore = ₹5. The other figures misplace the decimal or confuse profit with share count.
A share trades at ₹300 and its book value per share is ₹120. What is its price-to-book ratio?
0.4 times
3.0 times
2.5 times
1.8 times
P/B = market price ÷ book value per share = 300 ÷ 120 = 2.5. A ratio of 0.4 would result from dividing book value by price, which inverts the formula.
An investor prefers companies trading at low P/E and P/B ratios relative to their fundamentals. Her investment style is:
Growth investing
Value investing
Momentum investing
Index investing

Value investors seek stocks priced below their intrinsic worth, often indicated by low valuation multiples. Growth investors pay higher multiples for fast earnings growth, and momentum investors follow price trends.
A company splits its shares from face value ₹10 to ₹5. An investor held 200 shares at ₹800. Ignoring market movement, after the split she holds:
200 shares at about ₹400
400 shares at about ₹800
100 shares at about ₹1,600
400 shares at about ₹400
A 2-for-1 split doubles the share count and halves the price, leaving total value unchanged at ₹1,60,000. It does not change her proportionate ownership.
Which of the following is the main source of long-term return for equity investors?
Fixed interest paid by the company every quarter
Guaranteed repayment of capital on a maturity date
Growth in company earnings and dividends
Interest credited by the stock exchange
Equity returns come from dividends and price appreciation driven by earnings growth. Equity has no fixed interest or maturity, and exchanges do not pay interest to shareholders.
Which risk of equity investing cannot be removed by holding many stocks across sectors?
Company-specific management risk
Market risk
Risk of a single factory fire
Risk of one firm losing a key contract

Systematic or market risk affects all stocks, for example from interest rates or economic slowdown, and cannot be diversified away. Events specific to one company are unsystematic and can be diversified.
A shareholder bought a share at ₹400, received a dividend of ₹10 and sold it after one year at ₹440. What was his total return?
Total return = (price gain + dividend) ÷ purchase price = (40 + 10) ÷ 400 = 12.5%. 10% counts only the price gain and 2.5% only the dividend yield.
Under SEBI's categorisation, mid-cap companies are those ranked:
1st to 100th by full market capitalisation
251st onwards by full market capitalisation
1st to 50th by free-float market capitalisation
101st to 250th by full market capitalisation
SEBI defines large caps as the top 100 companies, mid caps as 101st to 250th and small caps as 251st onwards, ranked by full market capitalisation using AMFI's periodic list.

Debt Investment.overview: This chapter covers debt securities: features of bonds and debentures, coupon, face value, maturity, yield measures, the inverse price-yield relationship, duration, credit ratings and the main risks such as interest rate, credit, reinvestment and liquidity risk. It also covers government securities, corporate bonds, tax-free bonds and small savings. When revising, practise pricing a simple bond, compare yields, and match debt instruments to client needs based on horizon, risk and liquidity.
questions: A 3-year bond with face value ₹100 pays a 7% annual coupon. If the market yield for such bonds is 8%, its price is closest to:
Price = present value of coupons and principal at 8%: 7/1.08 + 7/1.08² + 107/1.08³ ≈ ₹97.42. When yield exceeds coupon, the bond trades at a discount; ₹102.67 is the price at a 6% yield.
Which bond will be most sensitive to a change in interest rates, other things equal?
A 20-year zero-coupon bond
A 2-year bond with a high coupon
A 91-day treasury bill
A 5-year floating rate bond reset every quarter

Price sensitivity rises with maturity and falls with coupon size. A long zero-coupon bond has the highest duration, so its price moves most. Floating rate bonds reset coupons and have low interest rate sensitivity.
The difference between the yield on a AA-rated corporate bond and a government security of similar maturity mainly reflects:
The inflation rate in the economy
The face value of the two bonds
The tax deducted on government securities
Credit and liquidity risk
The credit spread compensates investors for the corporate issuer's default risk and usually lower liquidity. Both bonds face the same inflation environment, so inflation does not explain the spread.
A bondholder receives coupons and must reinvest them at lower rates because interest rates have fallen. This is:
Credit risk
Default risk
Reinvestment risk
Liquidity risk
Reinvestment risk is the risk that intermediate cash flows will be reinvested at lower rates than expected, reducing realised returns. It rises when rates fall, the opposite of price risk.
A credit rating of 'AAA' on a bond indicates:
A guarantee by the government of repayment
That the bond will never fall in price
The highest degree of safety on timely servicing
That the issuer is a public sector company
AAA denotes the highest safety regarding timely payment of interest and principal, in the rating agency's opinion. It is not a guarantee, and the bond's price can still change with interest rates.
An upward-sloping yield curve means that:
Longer maturities have higher yields
Short-term yields are higher than long-term yields
All maturities carry the same yield
Bond prices always rise over time
A normal or upward-sloping yield curve shows higher yields for longer maturities, reflecting term premium and expectations. An inverted curve has short-term yields above long-term yields.
A conservative client wants regular income with minimal credit risk for five years. Which option best fits?
Unrated debentures of a small company
Perpetual bonds of a weak bank
A sector equity fund
Government securities of about five years

G-secs carry sovereign backing with negligible credit risk and pay regular coupons. Unrated or perpetual bonds of weak issuers carry significant credit risk, and equity funds do not offer stable income.
If market yields fall after a client buys a fixed-coupon bond, the bond's market price will:
Fall
Rise
Remain unchanged
Become zero
Bond prices move inversely to yields. When yields fall, existing bonds with higher coupons become more valuable, so their prices rise.

Derivatives.overview: This chapter introduces derivatives for an investment adviser: forwards, futures, options and swaps, their payoffs and their use in hedging and portfolio management. It covers margins, leverage, option terms such as strike, premium, intrinsic value and moneyness, and simple strategies like protective puts and covered calls. When revising, focus on how derivatives can reduce or increase risk, compute simple payoffs, and be able to judge whether a derivative strategy is suitable for a given client.
questions: A client holds shares at ₹800 and buys a put with strike ₹760 for ₹15. If the share falls to ₹650 at expiry, his net loss per share including premium is:
The put limits the sale price to ₹760, so the stock loss is 800 − 760 = ₹40, plus the ₹15 premium = ₹55. Without the put, the loss would have been ₹150.
Why is futures trading considered leveraged?
Only a margin is paid for the full exposure
The exchange lends shares to every trader free of cost
Futures prices cannot move more than 1% a day
The full contract value must be paid upfront in cash
With futures, a margin that is a fraction of contract value gives exposure to the full value, so small price moves cause large gains or losses relative to the money deposited.
An interest rate swap typically involves:
Buying shares in exchange for bonds
Converting rupees into dollars at a fixed rate permanently
Exchanging fixed-rate for floating-rate payments
Swapping one mutual fund scheme for another
In a plain interest rate swap, one party pays a fixed rate and the other a floating rate on a notional amount, with only net interest exchanged. It helps manage interest rate exposure.
A call option with strike ₹1,000 when the stock is at ₹1,080 is:
Out of the money
At the money
Worthless at any time
In the money
A call is in the money when the spot price exceeds the strike, since exercise would buy below market. Here intrinsic value is ₹80.
A client with no shares sells call options to earn premium. What is his risk?
Loss limited to the premium received
Potentially unlimited losses if the stock rises
No risk, since he receives money upfront
Loss limited to the strike price
A naked call writer must deliver at the strike if exercised, so losses grow without limit as the stock rises. The premium received is his maximum gain, not his maximum loss.
For a retail client seeking capital protection, an adviser considering derivatives should first check:
Which derivative offers the highest leverage
The latest tips on social media
Whether the client understands and can bear the risks
Whether the broker offers free trades
Suitability requires that the client understands the product and can bear potential losses. Leverage, tips or brokerage offers are not appropriate grounds for recommending derivatives.
An investor sells index futures against a diversified portfolio. If the market rises sharply, the futures position will:
Lose money, offsetting portfolio gains
Gain money, adding to portfolio gains
Be unaffected by market movement
Be automatically closed by SEBI
A short futures hedge loses when the market rises, offsetting gains on the portfolio. Hedging reduces both downside and upside, locking in the current value.
A forward contract differs from a futures contract in that a forward is:
Traded on an exchange with daily margins
Always settled in cash through a clearing corporation
Available only on stock indices
A private, customised OTC agreement
Forwards are bilateral and customised, with counterparty risk and no daily margining. Futures are standardised, exchange-traded and cleared by a clearing corporation.

Mutual Funds.overview: This chapter covers mutual funds as investment vehicles: structure (sponsor, trustee, AMC, custodian), scheme types under SEBI's categorisation, NAV, expense ratio, loads, direct and regular plans, SIPs, STPs and SWPs, risk-o-meter and taxation basics. Advisers must match schemes to client goals. When revising, compute redemption amounts and units, understand rupee cost averaging, know the main features of equity, debt, hybrid, index and solution-oriented schemes, and learn how to read a scheme's risk and cost information.
questions: A scheme's NAV is ₹50 and it has an exit load of 1% on redemptions within a year. An investor redeems within the year. What is the redemption price per unit?
Exit load is deducted from NAV: 50 × (1 − 0.01) = ₹49.50. ₹50.50 wrongly adds the load, which would apply to an entry load, now not charged by mutual funds.
An investor invests ₹6,000 each month for three months at NAVs of ₹20, ₹25 and ₹30. What is his average cost per unit?
About ₹26.10
About ₹24.32
Units bought = 300 + 240 + 200 = 740. Average cost = 18,000 ÷ 740 ≈ ₹24.32. This is below the simple average NAV of ₹25, illustrating rupee cost averaging.
Under SEBI's scheme categorisation, a multi cap fund must invest at least:
65% in large-cap stocks only
25% each in large, mid and small caps
80% in a single sector
50% in debt and 50% in equity
SEBI requires multi cap funds to hold at least 25% each in large-, mid- and small-cap stocks, ensuring true diversification across market caps. Flexi cap funds have no such minimums.
A client wants to move money from a liquid fund into an equity fund in equal monthly instalments. Which facility suits this?
Systematic transfer plan
Systematic withdrawal plan
Dividend reinvestment option
New fund offer
An STP periodically transfers a fixed amount from one scheme to another of the same fund house, spreading equity entry over time. An SWP pays money out to the investor.
Who holds the assets of a mutual fund scheme in safe custody?
The custodian
The asset management company
The sponsor
The registrar and transfer agent
The custodian, registered with SEBI, holds the scheme's securities. The AMC manages the money, the trustees oversee the AMC, and the RTA maintains unitholder records.
Equity linked savings schemes have a lock-in period of:
1 year
5 years
No lock-in at all
3 years
ELSS units are locked in for three years from the date of each investment, including each SIP instalment. They carry the shortest lock-in among tax-saving investment options under the old regime.
An arbitrage fund earns returns mainly from:
Long-term bets on small-cap stocks
Price gaps between cash and futures markets
Investing in foreign real estate
Lending to unrated companies
Arbitrage funds buy in the cash market and sell in futures (or vice versa) to capture the spread, giving low-risk, money-market-like returns while being treated as equity-oriented for tax.
The riskometer on a mutual fund scheme is meant to show:
The guaranteed return of the scheme
The fund manager's personal rating
The scheme's level of risk to investors
The number of investors in the scheme
The riskometer grades a scheme's risk from low to very high based on its portfolio and is reviewed monthly. It does not indicate returns or fund manager quality.

Real Estate, Gold & Other Assets.overview: This chapter covers alternative and real assets for individual investors: residential and commercial real estate, REITs and InvITs, gold in physical and financial forms (ETFs, funds, sovereign gold bonds), silver ETFs and other assets. Key themes are liquidity, costs, valuation, rental yields and diversification benefits. When revising, compare direct property with REITs, physical gold with gold ETFs, and think about how much of a client's portfolio should go into such assets and why.
questions: A flat bought for ₹80 lakh earns annual rent of ₹2.4 lakh. What is its gross rental yield?
Gross rental yield = annual rent ÷ property value = 2.4 lakh ÷ 80 lakh = 3%. Residential yields in Indian cities are often low, so returns depend heavily on capital appreciation.
Compared with buying commercial property directly, investing in a listed REIT offers:
Guaranteed rental income every month
Smaller ticket size and better liquidity
Complete control over the building's management
No exposure to real estate market risk
REIT units can be bought in small amounts and traded on exchanges, giving diversification across properties. Income is not guaranteed and unitholders still bear real estate risk.
An InvIT mainly holds:
Residential flats rented to individuals
Gold bars held in bank vaults
Infrastructure assets such as roads and power lines
Shares of listed IT companies
Infrastructure Investment Trusts own revenue-generating infrastructure assets like toll roads, transmission lines and pipelines. REITs hold real estate, and gold or shares are held by other vehicles.
Why is gold often included in a diversified portfolio?
It pays a high regular dividend
It is guaranteed to beat inflation every year
Its price never falls in rupee terms
It tends to have low correlation with equities
Gold often behaves differently from equities, especially in crises, so a modest allocation can reduce portfolio volatility. It pays no income on its own and its price can fall.
A key drawback of direct real estate as an investment is:
Its price is quoted every second on exchanges
Illiquidity and high transaction costs
It cannot be used as collateral for loans
It always gives lower returns than bank deposits
Property takes time to sell, needs large amounts and attracts stamp duty, registration and brokerage costs. These features reduce flexibility compared with financial assets.
Gold ETFs in India are backed by:
Shares of gold mining companies only
Bank fixed deposits
Government securities
Physical gold of specified purity
Gold ETFs hold physical gold of prescribed purity, and their NAV tracks domestic gold prices. Funds investing in mining companies are equity funds, not gold ETFs.
A client wants gold exposure without storage worries and with exchange liquidity. Which product fits best?
A gold exchange traded fund
Gold jewellery from a local shop
Gold coins kept in a home locker
A gold loan from an NBFC
Gold ETFs are held in demat form, avoid making charges and storage risk, and can be traded on exchanges. A gold loan is borrowing against gold, not an investment.
SEBI requires REITs to invest most of their assets in:
Undeveloped agricultural land
Listed equity shares of any sector
Completed, revenue-generating properties
Foreign currency deposits
SEBI regulations require the bulk of a REIT's value (at least 80%) to be in completed and rent-generating properties, limiting development risk. This supports stable distributions.

PMS, AIF & Other Managed Portfolios.overview: This chapter covers managed investment products beyond mutual funds: portfolio management services (discretionary, non-discretionary and advisory), alternative investment funds (Categories I, II and III), and newer options such as specialised investment funds. Learn their regulatory framework, minimum investment, structure, fees, taxation basics, transparency and suitability for high-net-worth investors. When revising, compare these products with mutual funds on cost, flexibility, risk, and liquidity, and know which AIF categories may use leverage.
questions: In a portfolio management service, the client's securities are held:
In the portfolio manager's proprietary account
In a pooled account like a mutual fund
In the client's own demat account
With the stock exchange as collateral
PMS portfolios are held individually in the client's name, giving full transparency and individual ownership. Mutual funds pool money and investors hold units, not the underlying securities.
Which AIF category can use leverage and employ complex trading strategies, including hedge funds?
Category I
Category III
Category II
None, AIFs cannot use leverage

Category III AIFs, such as hedge funds, may use leverage and complex strategies subject to limits. Category I invests in socially or economically desirable areas, and Category II includes private equity and debt funds without leverage for investment.
In a non-discretionary PMS, investment decisions are made:
By the manager only with client approval
Entirely by the portfolio manager without consulting the client
By SEBI on behalf of the client
Automatically by an index-tracking algorithm
In a non-discretionary PMS, the manager recommends and executes trades only after the client approves them. In a discretionary PMS, the manager decides on the client's behalf.
Category I AIFs include funds that invest in:
Listed derivatives with high leverage
Only government securities
Only gold and silver
Start-ups, SMEs and infrastructure
Category I AIFs include venture capital, angel, SME and infrastructure funds that the government considers economically or socially desirable. Leveraged trading strategies fall under Category III.
Compared with a mutual fund, a PMS generally offers:
More customisation at a higher minimum
Lower minimum investment and pooled ownership
Guaranteed returns approved by SEBI
Daily NAV published on AMFI's website
PMS offers a personalised portfolio with individual holdings, but has a high minimum ticket and often performance-linked fees. Mutual funds are pooled, have low minimums and publish daily NAVs.
A Category II AIF that invests in unlisted companies is best described as:
A liquid mutual fund
A private equity fund
A government bond fund
An index exchange traded fund
Private equity and private debt funds are typical Category II AIFs investing in unlisted companies or instruments. Liquid funds, G-sec funds and ETFs are mutual fund products.
Why are PMS and AIF products generally suitable only for wealthier, experienced investors?
They are banned for residents of India
They do not allow any investment in equity
They need large tickets and carry higher risk
They are guaranteed by the government
High minimum investments, concentrated or complex strategies and limited liquidity make these products suitable mainly for investors with large portfolios and the ability to bear losses.
A portfolio manager reports performance to clients. SEBI requires PMS performance to be reported using:
Only the return in the best month
The return before any fees and expenses
A simple average of yearly returns
A time-weighted rate of return
SEBI requires PMS returns to be computed on a time-weighted basis, net of fees and expenses, and compared with a benchmark, allowing fair comparison across managers.

Asset Allocation & Portfolio Constructio.overview: This chapter covers asset allocation as the main driver of portfolio outcomes: strategic, tactical and dynamic allocation, risk and return of portfolios, correlation and diversification, core-satellite construction, rebalancing, and the investment policy statement. When revising, practise calculating portfolio return and risk, understand how correlation affects diversification, and be able to propose an allocation from a client's goals, horizon and risk profile and explain when and how to rebalance.
questions: A portfolio has 60% in asset A (standard deviation 20%) and 40% in asset B (standard deviation 8%), with a correlation of 0.2. Its standard deviation is closest to:
σp = √(0.6²×0.2² + 0.4²×0.08² + 2×0.6×0.4×0.2×0.08×0.2) ≈ 13.0%. 15.2% is the weighted average, which applies only with perfect correlation.
In a core-satellite approach, the 'core' is usually invested in:
Low-cost, diversified funds
Highly concentrated small-cap bets
Frequent trading in options
A single sector expected to boom
The core holds broad, low-cost investments that capture market returns reliably. Satellites are smaller positions in active or thematic ideas that aim for extra returns.
An investment policy statement (IPS) mainly records:
Daily market tips given to the client
Objectives, constraints and allocation policy
Only the adviser's fee invoice
The client's tax return for the year
The IPS documents the client's goals, risk tolerance, time horizon, liquidity and other constraints, target allocation and review rules. It guides decisions and keeps both parties disciplined.
Which client is most suited to a higher equity allocation?
A 75-year-old retiree living off portfolio income
A client needing the money for a house in one year
A client with no emergency fund and unstable income
A 30-year-old with stable income and long goals
A long horizon and stable income increase capacity to bear equity volatility. Short horizons, reliance on portfolio income and lack of buffers argue for lower equity.
Dynamic asset allocation differs from strategic allocation because it:
Never changes once set at the start
Invests only in fixed deposits
Is used only by government pension funds
Changes the mix based on market conditions
Dynamic allocation shifts between equity and debt in response to valuations or other signals. Strategic allocation is a long-term target mix maintained by periodic rebalancing.
Calendar rebalancing means a portfolio is rebalanced:
At fixed intervals, such as yearly
Only when the client asks for a new product
Whenever the market moves by 1% in a day
Never, to save transaction costs
Calendar rebalancing resets the portfolio to target weights at regular intervals. Threshold rebalancing instead triggers when weights drift beyond set bands.
Adding an asset with negative correlation to an existing portfolio is likely to:
Increase overall portfolio volatility sharply
Reduce overall portfolio volatility
Have no effect on portfolio risk
Guarantee a higher return
Negatively correlated assets tend to move in opposite directions, smoothing portfolio returns and lowering volatility. Diversification does not guarantee higher returns.
A client's risk profile suggests 50% equity, but she wants 90% equity after hearing friends' stories. The adviser should:
Immediately raise equity to 90% to keep her happy
Refuse to advise her any further
Explain the risks and stick to a suitable allocation
Move everything into a single hot stock
Advisers must recommend suitable allocations and educate clients on risks. Changing the allocation purely due to peer influence would breach suitability; refusing to engage helps no one.

Portfolio Performance Evaluation.overview: This chapter covers how to measure and judge portfolio performance: holding period return, time-weighted and money-weighted returns, annualisation, benchmarks, and risk-adjusted measures such as Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen's alpha, Sortino and information ratio, along with tracking error. When revising, practise each formula with numbers, understand which measure suits a diversified versus concentrated portfolio, and learn why returns must always be compared with a suitable benchmark and adjusted for risk.
questions: A fund returned 12% when the risk-free rate was 6%. Its downside deviation was 8%. What is its Sortino ratio?
Sortino ratio = (portfolio return − risk-free rate) ÷ downside deviation = (12 − 6) ÷ 8 = 0.75. Unlike Sharpe, it penalises only downside volatility.
A fund beat its benchmark by 2% a year with a tracking error of 4%. What is its information ratio?
Information ratio = active return ÷ tracking error = 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5. It measures how consistently a manager adds return over the benchmark per unit of active risk.
Which return measure removes the effect of the timing of investor cash flows and is preferred for judging a fund manager?
Money-weighted return
Simple absolute return
Dividend yield
Time-weighted return

Time-weighted return links sub-period returns, so it is not distorted by when investors add or withdraw money, which the manager does not control. Money-weighted return (IRR) reflects the investor's own timing.
For a well-diversified portfolio, which risk-adjusted measure uses beta as the measure of risk?
Sharpe ratio
Treynor ratio
Sortino ratio
Information ratio
The Treynor ratio divides excess return by beta, focusing on systematic risk, which is appropriate when unsystematic risk has been diversified away. Sharpe uses total standard deviation.
An investment gave a return of 21% over two years. Its annualised (compound) return is closest to:
Annualised return = (1.21)^(1/2) − 1 = 10%. Dividing 21% by two gives 10.5%, which ignores compounding and overstates the yearly rate.
Why must a mid-cap fund be compared with a mid-cap index rather than the Nifty 50?
The benchmark must match the fund's universe
The Nifty 50 is not a valid index
Mid-cap indices always give higher returns
SEBI bans comparison with large-cap indices
A benchmark should reflect the fund's investment universe and risk. Comparing a mid-cap fund with a large-cap index mixes style effects with manager skill.
Tracking error of an index fund measures:
The fund's expense ratio
The index's average return
The number of stocks in the index
Volatility of the fund's return gap
Tracking error is the standard deviation of the difference between fund and index returns, showing how consistently the fund replicates its benchmark. Lower is better for an index fund.
Two funds have equal returns. Fund X has a higher standard deviation than Fund Y. Based on the Sharpe ratio:
Fund X has better risk-adjusted return
Fund Y has better risk-adjusted return
Both have identical risk-adjusted returns
The Sharpe ratio cannot compare them
With the same excess return, the fund with lower standard deviation has a higher Sharpe ratio. Fund Y delivered the same return for less total risk.

Behavioural Finance.overview: This chapter explains how psychology affects investment decisions. It covers heuristics and biases such as anchoring, mental accounting, overconfidence, herding, loss aversion, confirmation bias, framing, home bias and endowment effect, and the limits of the efficient-markets view. Advisers must recognise these biases in clients and in themselves and use process, education and goal-based planning to reduce costly mistakes. When revising, match each bias to a typical client statement or behaviour.
questions: A client refuses to sell a stock until it returns to the price he paid, ₹500, although its prospects have changed. This shows:
Herding
Home bias
Anchoring
Overconfidence
Anchoring is fixation on a reference point, here the purchase price, which is irrelevant to the stock's future value. Decisions should be based on current prospects.
A client treats her bonus as 'fun money' and spends it on speculative trades while keeping her salary savings very conservative. This is:
Loss aversion
Recency bias
Status quo bias
Mental accounting
Mental accounting is treating money differently depending on its source or label, although all rupees are interchangeable. A unified portfolio view leads to better decisions.
Investors rush to buy a theme because everyone around them is buying it. This behaviour is:
Anchoring
Herding
Framing
Endowment effect
Herding is following the crowd instead of independent analysis, which can inflate bubbles. It often leads to buying near peaks and selling near troughs.
A trader believes his stock picks are far better than average and trades very frequently. This reflects:
Overconfidence
Mental accounting
Loss aversion
Home bias
Overconfident investors overrate their knowledge and skill, leading to excessive trading and under-diversification, which tends to reduce net returns after costs.
A client reads only news that supports his view that a stock will rise and ignores negative reports. This is:
Recency bias
Anchoring
Herding
Confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is seeking information that confirms existing beliefs and ignoring contrary evidence. Advisers can counter it by presenting balanced analysis.
A client prefers a plan described as having a '90% chance of meeting the goal' over one with a '10% chance of failing', though they are identical. This is:
Mental accounting
Overconfidence
Framing
Disposition effect
Framing means decisions change with how identical information is presented. Advisers should present information neutrally and in several ways so the client's choice is not driven by wording.
Loss aversion means that investors:
Feel losses more than equal gains
Prefer losses to gains of the same size
Are indifferent between gains and losses
Avoid all equity investments by law
Prospect theory shows a loss hurts roughly twice as much as an equal gain pleases. This can make investors overly cautious or reluctant to realise losses.
Which adviser action best helps clients avoid behavioural mistakes during a market crash?
Switching the whole portfolio to cash immediately
Revisiting the goal-based plan
Recommending a new hot sector fund
Avoiding any contact until markets recover
Reminding clients of their long-term goals, allocation and past recoveries reduces panic selling. Knee-jerk moves or silence tend to worsen outcomes.

Operational Aspects (KYC, Demat, Transac.overview: This chapter covers the operational side of investing: KYC requirements, KYC Registration Agencies and the Central KYC registry, in-person and video verification, PAN and Aadhaar, nomination, demat accounts and depository participants, basic services demat accounts, transaction processes in mutual funds and securities, and change of details. When revising, know what documents are needed, who maintains KYC records, how nomination works, and the steps and timelines for common transactions.
questions: The Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR) is maintained by:
SEBI
CERSAI
NSDL
AMFI

CKYCR is operated by the Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India (CERSAI), allowing one KYC to be used across financial sectors. NSDL is a depository and AMFI is an industry body.
A basic services demat account (BSDA) is meant for:
Institutional investors only
Foreign portfolio investors
Companies issuing shares
Small investors with low holdings
BSDA offers lower or nil annual maintenance charges to individuals with small holdings below a threshold, encouraging financial inclusion. Other accounts carry normal charges.
Why should an investor add a nominee to a demat account?
To allow the nominee to trade freely now
To reduce tax on dividends
To ease transfer of holdings on death
To increase the account's credit limit
Nomination lets securities be transmitted smoothly to the nominee after the holder's death. It does not give the nominee trading rights during the holder's lifetime or affect tax.
A client changes his address. Updating it once with the KRA ensures that:
All linked intermediaries get the update
Only his bank account is updated
His PAN is cancelled and reissued
His existing investments are redeemed
KRAs share KYC data with registered intermediaries, so one update flows to mutual funds, brokers and others using that KYC. PAN and investments are unaffected.
Which document is mandatory for most securities market transactions in India?
Passport
Voter ID
PAN
Driving licence
PAN is the key identifier for securities market transactions, with limited exemptions. Other documents may serve as address proof but are not mandatory identifiers.
A client wants to convert physical share certificates into electronic form. This process is:
Dematerialisation
Rematerialisation
Transmission
Pledging
Dematerialisation converts physical certificates into electronic holdings through a DP. Rematerialisation is the reverse, transmission is transfer on death, and pledging creates a charge.
In-person verification during KYC can now be done through:
A phone call without video
An email with a scanned signature only
A newspaper advertisement
Video-based verification
SEBI permits video-based in-person verification by intermediaries, using secure processes, as an alternative to physical meetings. Phone calls or emails alone do not meet IPV norms.
A mutual fund unitholder submits a redemption request. The AMC must normally pay the money within:
Ten working days
Three working days
One calendar month
Fifteen working days
SEBI and AMFI norms require redemption proceeds to be paid within three working days for most schemes, with interest for delays. Some exceptional cases allow longer timelines.

Regulatory Framework for Investment Advi.overview: This chapter covers the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 as amended: who must register, exemptions, qualification and certification, segregation of advisory and distribution, client agreements, risk profiling and suitability, fee modes, disclosures, record keeping and audit. Rules are revised periodically, so focus on principles: an adviser is paid only by clients, must keep advice independent of distribution, must profile risk and recommend suitable products, and must keep records and disclose conflicts.
questions: A registered investment adviser wants to also distribute mutual funds to the same client and earn commissions. Under SEBI's framework this is:
Allowed if the adviser waives her advisory fee
Allowed for clients with small portfolios
Allowed if disclosed only after the sale
Not allowed, as advice and distribution are segregated
SEBI requires client-level segregation of advisory and distribution so that an adviser does not earn commissions from products she recommends. Waiving fees does not cure the conflict.
Before giving advice, a registered investment adviser must enter into:
A written agreement with the client
An agreement with the fund house
An arrangement with a stock broker
A contract with the stock exchange
IA Regulations require a client agreement covering terms, fees, scope and disclosures before advisory services begin. Arrangements with product providers would create conflicts.
Which fee arrangement is permitted for a SEBI-registered investment adviser?
Commission from mutual fund houses
A share of insurance premiums
A fixed fee or a fee based on assets
Brokerage on trades the client places
SEBI allows advisers to charge either a fixed fee or a fee linked to assets under advice, within prescribed limits, from the client only. Commissions and brokerage are not permitted.
Investment advisers must conduct risk profiling to:
Decide which product pays the highest fee
Ensure advice suits the client's risk
Fulfil a tax filing requirement
Rank clients by income for marketing
Risk profiling assesses a client's capacity and willingness to take risk, so advice can be matched to it. It is a core suitability requirement, not a marketing or tax tool.
An adviser's recommended scheme can be bought by the client through:
Regular plans that pay the adviser commission
Any plan, as long as the client signs a waiver
Only through the adviser's own trading account
Direct plans with no commission
Advisers implementing advice must use direct plans or commission-free routes, since they cannot earn distribution income. Using regular plans would breach segregation norms.
Which of the following is an obligation of a registered investment adviser?
Guaranteeing returns on recommended products
Maintaining records of advice and its basis
Sharing client data with distributors
Holding client funds in its own bank account
Advisers must keep records of client profiles, advice given and the rationale for the prescribed period. They may not guarantee returns, share data improperly or handle client funds.
An insurance agent who gives advice only on insurance products sold by him needs to register as an investment adviser?
No, such advice is exempt
Yes, under all circumstances
Yes, if he sells more than ten policies a year
Only if he advises on term insurance
IA Regulations exempt insurance agents and brokers who offer advice only on insurance products regulated by IRDAI. Advising on securities would require registration.
Who regulates and supervises registered investment advisers on behalf of SEBI through a recognised body?
AMFI
NSDL
BSE Administration and Supervision Ltd
The Insurance Ombudsman
SEBI has recognised BSE Administration and Supervision Limited (BASL), a BSE subsidiary, as the body to administer and supervise investment advisers. AMFI is a mutual fund industry body.

Ethics, Conflicts & Grievance Redressal.overview: This chapter covers the ethical duties of an investment adviser: acting in the client's best interest, avoiding or disclosing conflicts of interest, confidentiality, fair dealing, avoiding misrepresentation and maintaining professional competence. It also covers the investor grievance mechanism, including handling complaints within set timelines, SEBI SCORES and the online dispute resolution platform. When revising, apply principles to scenarios: identify the conflict, decide what must be disclosed or avoided, and know the correct path for escalating complaints.
questions: An adviser receives a gift voucher from a fund house whose schemes she recommends. What should she do?
Accept it quietly as a normal business gift
Recommend that fund house's schemes more often
Decline it or disclose it as a conflict
Share the voucher with the client to balance it
Benefits from product providers create conflicts that can bias advice. The adviser should avoid such benefits or at least disclose them; increasing recommendations would worsen the breach.
An adviser shares a client's portfolio details with a property developer without consent. This breaches:
Diversification norms
Client confidentiality
Asset allocation policy
Rupee cost averaging
Client information must be kept confidential and used only for advisory purposes unless consent is given or law requires disclosure. Sharing it with a developer is a serious breach.
A client complains to an adviser. Within what broad expectation should the adviser respond?
Promptly, within prescribed timelines
Only when SEBI asks the adviser to respond
After the client's next annual review
Never, if the adviser thinks the complaint is wrong
Advisers must have a grievance redressal mechanism and resolve complaints within SEBI's prescribed timelines. Unresolved complaints can be escalated by the client to SCORES and ODR.
An adviser holds shares of a company she is about to recommend to clients. The ethical approach is to:
Recommend it without mentioning her holding
Buy more shares before recommending it
Sell her shares just after clients buy
Disclose her holding to clients
Personal holdings in recommended securities are a conflict that must be disclosed, and trading around recommendations is improper. Clients need to know of any interest that may affect advice.
An adviser realises she lacks expertise in a client's complex cross-border tax issue. She should:
Give a confident answer to keep the client
Ignore the issue in the plan
Copy advice from an online forum
Refer the client to a qualified expert
Professional competence means knowing one's limits and seeking expert help where needed. Guessing or ignoring material issues can harm the client.
If an investor's complaint is not resolved through SCORES, a further option is:
The Banking Ombudsman
SEBI's online dispute resolution platform
The Income Tax department
The Competition Commission of India
SEBI's ODR platform offers online conciliation and arbitration for unresolved securities market disputes. The banking ombudsman, tax department and CCI do not handle such disputes.
Showing a client only the best-performing period of a recommended fund, while hiding weaker periods, is:
Acceptable marketing practice
Required by SEBI for clarity
Misleading and unethical
Fine if the client is a high-net-worth investor
Selective presentation of performance misrepresents the product. Advisers must present balanced, fair information covering appropriate periods, risks and benchmarks.
Fair treatment of clients requires that an adviser:
Does not favour some clients over others
Gives the best ideas only to the largest clients
Charges different fees without disclosure
Allocates scarce opportunities to family members first
Fair dealing means treating all clients equitably in advice and allocation, with transparent fees. Favouring large clients or family members breaches this duty.

Risk Management & Insurance Concepts.overview: This chapter introduces personal risk management and the principles of insurance. It covers identifying risks, methods of handling them (avoidance, reduction, retention and transfer), pooling of risk, and legal principles such as utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity, subrogation, contribution and proximate cause. When revising, match each principle to a claim scenario, understand why some risks are better retained and others transferred, and know how insurance fits into a client's overall financial plan.
questions: A client keeps a large emergency fund to meet small medical bills himself instead of buying a low-deductible policy. This method of handling risk is:
Risk avoidance
Risk transfer
Risk elimination
Risk retention
Bearing small, predictable losses from one's own resources is risk retention. Insurance would be risk transfer, while avoidance means not undertaking the risky activity at all.
After paying a car damage claim, an insurer recovers the amount from the third party who caused the accident. This is based on the principle of:
Contribution
Utmost good faith
Subrogation
Insurable interest
Subrogation lets the insurer, after paying a claim, step into the insured's shoes to recover from the party responsible. It prevents the insured from being paid twice.
A house worth ₹50 lakh is insured with two insurers for ₹50 lakh each. A fire causes ₹10 lakh of damage. Under the principle of contribution, the owner can recover:
₹10 lakh in total, shared by insurers
₹20 lakh, ₹10 lakh from each insurer
₹10 lakh from each insurer separately
Nothing, because double insurance is illegal
Contribution ensures the insured recovers only the actual loss, with insurers sharing it rateably. Indemnity prevents profit from insurance, so ₹20 lakh cannot be recovered.
Which risk is generally considered insurable?
Loss from a fall in share prices
Accidental fire damage to a factory
Loss due to a business decision going wrong
A certain loss that will definitely happen
Insurable risks are pure, accidental, measurable and affect many similar exposures. Speculative risks like share price falls and certain losses are not insurable.
Pooling of risk in insurance works because:
Every policyholder is guaranteed to make a claim
The insurer invests only in fixed deposits
Losses of a few are paid from many premiums
Premiums are refunded if no claim is made
Insurance pools premiums from many people facing similar risks; only some suffer losses, which are paid from the common fund. The law of large numbers makes losses predictable.
A client installs smoke detectors and fire extinguishers in his shop. This is an example of:
Risk transfer
Risk retention
Risk avoidance
Risk reduction
Taking steps to lower the likelihood or severity of a loss is risk reduction or loss control. It complements insurance but does not transfer the risk to an insurer.
A death occurred because an accident led to an injury that caused fatal infection. The principle used to decide whether the accident cover applies is:
Proximate cause
Indemnity
Contribution
Subrogation
Proximate cause identifies the dominant, effective cause in an unbroken chain of events. If the accident set the chain in motion, the accident cover typically responds.
Which statement about utmost good faith is correct?
Only the insurer must disclose facts
Both proposer and insurer must disclose material facts
Only facts asked in the form need disclosure
It applies only to motor insurance
Utmost good faith requires full disclosure of all material facts by both parties. Non-disclosure by the proposer can make the policy voidable, and insurers must also explain terms fairly.

Life Insurance Products.overview: This chapter covers the life insurance products an adviser must evaluate: term plans, endowment and money-back plans, whole life, unit linked insurance plans (ULIPs), pension and annuity plans, and riders. It also covers participating versus non-participating policies, surrender value, paid-up value, nomination and assignment, and the Married Women's Property Act protection. When revising, compare products on cost, cover and returns, and learn why pure term cover plus separate investments often suits clients best.
questions: Which life insurance policy provides cover for the whole of the insured's life rather than a fixed term?
Term insurance policy
Money-back policy
Whole life policy
Endowment policy of 15 years
A whole life policy covers the insured for life (often up to age 99 or 100), paying on death whenever it occurs. Term, money-back and endowment plans have fixed terms.
A participating (with-profit) policy differs from a non-participating policy because it:
Offers guaranteed returns linked to the stock market
Shares in the insurer's surplus via bonuses
Has no surrender value at any time
Cannot be bought by salaried individuals
Participating policies receive bonuses from the insurer's surplus, which are not guaranteed in advance. Non-participating policies offer only contracted benefits.
A policyholder transfers the rights under his life policy to a bank as security for a loan. This is called:
Assignment
Nomination
Surrender
Revival
Assignment transfers the policy's rights and benefits to another person or entity, such as a lender. A nominee only receives the claim money; ownership remains with the policyholder.
Which rider would pay an additional sum if the insured dies in an accident?
Waiver of premium rider
Critical illness rider
Hospital cash rider
Accidental death benefit rider
An accidental death benefit rider pays an extra amount if death is caused by an accident. A waiver of premium rider stops future premiums on specified events.
In a ULIP, the investment risk on the fund portion is borne by:
The policyholder
The insurance company
IRDAI
The fund manager personally
ULIP premiums, after charges, buy units whose value depends on market performance. The policyholder bears the investment risk, unlike guaranteed traditional plans.
A 30-year-old wants ₹1 crore of cover for 30 years at the lowest cost. Which product best meets this need?
Endowment plan
Whole life plan with bonuses
Money-back plan
Term insurance plan
Term insurance provides pure protection with no savings element, so premiums are far lower for the same cover. Endowment and money-back plans are much costlier per rupee of cover.
Under the free-look provision, a new life insurance policyholder can:
Get a full refund at any time during the term
Change the insurer without any formalities
Return the policy within the free-look period
Increase cover without medical tests
The free-look period lets a new policyholder review terms and cancel the policy for a refund, after deductions for proportionate risk premium and expenses. IRDAI has extended this period to 30 days.
A money-back policy is best described as a policy that:
Pays only if the insured survives to 100
Pays part of the sum assured at intervals
Returns all premiums if no claim is made
Pays the sum assured only on accidental death
A money-back policy pays survival benefits periodically during the term, with full sum assured payable on death. It is a variant of endowment assurance.

Health & General Insurance.overview: This chapter covers non-life insurance for individuals: health insurance (indemnity hospitalisation policies, family floaters, critical illness, top-up and super top-up covers), and general insurance such as motor, home and personal accident covers. Key concepts include sum insured, deductibles, co-payment, room-rent limits, waiting periods, pre-existing diseases, cashless claims and no-claim bonus. When revising, practise claim calculations with deductibles and co-payments and know how standard rules on waiting periods and portability protect policyholders.
questions: A top-up policy has a deductible of ₹5 lakh. A single hospital bill is ₹7 lakh. Ignoring other limits, how much will the top-up insurer pay?
₹7 lakh
₹5 lakh
₹2 lakh
Nothing
A top-up pays only the amount above the deductible for a single claim: 7 lakh − 5 lakh = ₹2 lakh. The first ₹5 lakh must be met by the base policy or the insured.
A critical illness policy differs from a hospitalisation policy because it:
Reimburses actual hospital bills only
Covers only outpatient consultation
Pays only if the insured dies
Pays a lump sum on diagnosis
Critical illness cover is a benefit policy paying a fixed sum on diagnosis of a listed illness, regardless of actual bills. Hospitalisation policies are indemnity covers.
Portability in health insurance allows a policyholder to:
Switch insurer while keeping waiting-period credit
Transfer the policy to a friend
Convert health cover into life cover
Claim from two insurers for the same bill
Portability lets a policyholder move to another insurer without losing credit for waiting periods already served. It does not allow transfer to another person or double recovery.
A no-claim bonus in health insurance usually results in:
A cash refund of all premiums paid
Higher sum insured after claim-free years
A lower deductible for life
Removal of all waiting periods
NCB rewards claim-free years, typically by increasing the sum insured (cumulative bonus) or lowering premium. It is not a refund of premiums.
A personal accident policy typically covers:
Hospital bills for any illness
Damage to the insured's car
Accidental death and disability
Theft of household goods
Personal accident covers pay for death and permanent or temporary disability caused by accidents. Illness, motor damage and burglary need other covers.
Under IRDAI's rules, the maximum waiting period that insurers can apply for pre-existing diseases in health policies is:
3 years
8 years
1 month
10 years
IRDAI's 2024 health insurance norms cap the waiting period for pre-existing diseases at three years. This replaced the earlier maximum of four years.
Which motor insurance cover pays for damage to the insured's own vehicle as well as third-party liability?
Third-party liability only policy
Personal accident cover for the owner-driver
Engine protection add-on alone
A comprehensive (package) policy
A comprehensive policy combines own-damage cover with mandatory third-party liability. A standalone third-party policy does not pay for damage to one's own vehicle.
A health policy has a room-rent limit of 1% of sum insured per day. Choosing a costlier room usually leads to:
The insurer paying the full bill anyway
Proportionate deduction from related charges
Automatic cancellation of the policy
A refund of the premium paid
With room-rent caps, insurers often reduce associated charges proportionately when a costlier room is taken, so the claim payout falls more than the room-rent difference.

Insurance Needs Analysis.overview: This chapter teaches how to estimate how much life, health and other insurance a client needs. It covers the human life value approach, the need-based (expense replacement) approach, and how to account for liabilities, goals, existing cover and assets. It also covers assessing health cover adequacy, disability needs and reviewing cover over the life cycle. When revising, practise needs calculations, understand when HLV and needs-based figures differ, and know the typical gaps in Indian households' insurance.
questions: A family's monthly expenses are ₹40,000 today. At 6% inflation, what will the same expenses cost per month in 20 years?
About ₹88,000
About ₹64,000
Future expense = 40,000 × 1.06^20 ≈ ₹1,28,285. ₹88,000 assumes simple growth of 6% a year. Inflation compounds, which is why needs analysis must project costs.
In a needs-based analysis, which item reduces the additional life cover required?
Outstanding home loan
Existing liquid investments and cover
Children's future education costs
Family's future living expenses
Required cover = liabilities + future needs − existing assets and insurance. Loans, education costs and expenses add to the need; existing resources reduce it.
Why does a young earner's insurance need usually fall as he approaches retirement?
Insurance premiums become tax-free after 50
Liabilities always increase with age
Life insurance cannot be bought after 50
Fewer years of income remain to protect
Insurance replaces future income; as remaining working years shrink and assets grow, the gap insurance must fill gets smaller. Liabilities usually fall with age.
A homemaker has no income. Why may she still need life insurance?
Insurers do not offer cover to homemakers
Her family would gain financially from her death
Her services would cost money to replace
Life cover is mandatory for all adults
Childcare, home management and other services have economic value that the family would need to pay for. Cover can be sized on this replacement cost.
A client has ₹20 lakh of group health cover from his employer. What is the main risk of relying on it alone?
Cover may end when he leaves the job
Group cover is never valid in hospitals
Group cover always excludes his spouse
Group cover can only be used outside India
Employer cover usually lapses on leaving the job or retiring, when buying fresh cover may be harder or costlier. A personal policy provides continuity.
Disability income insurance is meant to:
Pay for vehicle repairs after an accident
Repay home loans on job loss
Replace income lost due to disability
Fund children's education on death
Disability income cover pays a portion of income if illness or injury prevents the insured from working. It addresses a risk often more likely than early death.
Which approach to life insurance needs looks at the economic value of a person's future earnings?
Need-based approach
Rule of 72
Expense ratio method
Human life value approach
HLV estimates the present value of future income the person would contribute to the family. The need-based approach instead sums specific future needs and liabilities.
Which is the most appropriate first step when reviewing an existing client's life cover?
Surrender all existing policies immediately
Compare current cover with updated needs
Buy an additional endowment plan
Ignore cover once a policy is bought
A review recalculates needs considering changes in income, family, loans and assets, then compares them with existing cover to identify gaps. Surrendering policies hastily can be costly.

Retirement Planning Concepts.overview: This chapter covers the concepts behind retirement planning: phases of retirement, estimating retirement expenses, income replacement, inflation and longevity risk, sequence-of-returns risk, health costs and the need for a corpus that lasts. It also covers the impact of starting early and the trade-off between saving more, working longer and retiring later. When revising, practise projecting expenses, understand why real returns matter, and know the main risks a retiree faces.
questions: Why does starting retirement savings ten years earlier usually reduce the monthly saving required?
Inflation stops affecting long-term savings
Retirement expenses fall when one starts early
Government matches all early contributions
Money compounds for longer
A longer accumulation period lets returns compound for more years, so each rupee saved early grows more. Inflation and expenses are unaffected by when saving begins.
A client's current expenses are ₹30,000 a month and she retires in 25 years. At 6% inflation, her first-month retirement expense is closest to:
Future expense = 30,000 × 1.06^25 ≈ ₹1,28,756. ₹75,000 adds 6% simple growth each year and understates the effect of compounding inflation.
A retiree's corpus earns 7% while inflation is 7%. Her real rate of return is:
Zero
Negative 7%
Real return = (1.07 ÷ 1.07) − 1 = 0. The corpus grows only enough to keep pace with inflation, so withdrawals in real terms simply deplete principal.
Which retirement risk relates to rising medical costs with age?
Reinvestment risk
Healthcare cost risk
Currency risk
Credit risk
Healthcare costs tend to rise faster than general inflation and increase with age, so retirement plans should include adequate health cover and a medical reserve.
The accumulation phase of retirement planning refers to:
Years after retirement when the corpus is spent
The month of retirement only
Working years when the corpus is built
The period after the corpus is exhausted
During the accumulation phase, the client saves and invests to build the retirement corpus. The distribution phase starts at retirement, when the corpus funds expenses.
Which action would most reduce a client's required retirement corpus, all else equal?
Retiring earlier
Assuming higher inflation
Planning for a longer life expectancy
Retiring later
Retiring later shortens the retirement period and lengthens the saving period, reducing the corpus needed. Earlier retirement, higher inflation and longer life all raise it.
Why should retirement planning assume a life expectancy beyond the average?
Average life expectancy is fixed by law
Many people outlive the average
Insurers require it for every client
Corpus need falls with longer life
Average life expectancy means about half of people live longer. Planning to an older age protects against outliving savings, the core of longevity risk.
Expenses that typically fall after retirement include:
Commuting and work-related costs
Medical and health insurance costs
Leisure travel in early retirement
Domestic help as mobility reduces
Work-related costs such as commuting and work clothing usually fall after retirement, while health, leisure and assistance costs often rise.

Retirement Products & Pension Schemes.overview: This chapter covers the products used to save for retirement in India: Employees' Provident Fund and EPS, Voluntary Provident Fund, Public Provident Fund, the National Pension System (Tier I and Tier II), Atal Pension Yojana, annuity products, senior citizens' schemes and retirement-oriented mutual funds. Learn eligibility, contribution rules, lock-in, withdrawal and exit rules, and tax treatment in broad terms. Limits and exit rules are revised from time to time, so focus on structure and suitability.
questions: Under NPS, the subscriber's contributions are invested by:
The subscriber's employer directly
Banks as fixed deposits only
The Employees' Provident Fund Organisation
PFRDA-registered pension fund managers
NPS contributions are managed by pension fund managers regulated by PFRDA, across equity, corporate bonds, government securities and alternative assets as chosen by the subscriber.
The Voluntary Provident Fund allows a salaried employee to:
Contribute more than the mandatory EPF share
Withdraw EPF money every month
Invest EPF money in equity directly
Transfer EPF to his spouse's account
VPF lets employees contribute above the statutory EPF contribution, earning the EPF interest rate. The employer is not required to match the extra contribution.
An NPS subscriber can choose 'auto choice'. This means:
All money is invested only in equity
Asset mix changes with age
The subscriber picks stocks personally
Contributions are kept in a savings account
Under auto choice, NPS assets are allocated across asset classes according to a life-cycle fund, reducing equity exposure as the subscriber ages. Active choice lets the subscriber set the mix.
Which scheme is aimed mainly at workers in the unorganised sector, offering a guaranteed minimum pension?
Employees' Provident Fund
Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme
Atal Pension Yojana
Pradhan Mantri Vaya Vandana Yojana

APY offers a guaranteed minimum monthly pension after 60 depending on contribution, targeting unorganised sector workers. EPF is for organised sector employees and SCSS is a deposit scheme for seniors.
An immediate annuity bought with a lump sum at retirement:
Defers income for at least ten years
Pays only on death of the annuitant
Starts regular income straight away
Allows withdrawal of capital at any time
An immediate annuity converts a lump sum into regular income starting soon after purchase. A deferred annuity starts payments later, and annuities usually do not allow free capital withdrawal.
Employer contributions to EPF are split between EPF and the Employees' Pension Scheme. The EPS portion provides:
A monthly pension after retirement
A lump sum gratuity on resignation
Health cover for the family
Life insurance of a fixed amount
Part of the employer's contribution goes to EPS, which pays a monthly pension based on pensionable salary and service. EDLI provides insurance; gratuity is separate.
