Why might a retiree choose a 'joint life with return of purchase price' annuity?
Highest possible annuity rate for one person
No income until both spouses die
Guaranteed equity-linked returns
Income for both spouses, capital to heirs
This option pays income while either spouse lives and returns the purchase price to nominees after both die. The trade-off is a lower annuity rate than a single-life option.
A retirement-oriented mutual fund scheme under SEBI's solution-oriented category has a lock-in of:
No lock-in
Five years or till retirement, whichever is earlier
One year
Until age 75
SEBI's retirement funds are solution-oriented schemes with a lock-in of at least five years or until retirement age, whichever is earlier, encouraging long-term saving.

Retirement Corpus & Distribution Plannin.overview: This chapter covers how to calculate the corpus a client needs at retirement and how to draw it down safely. Topics include estimating first-year expenses, using real rates of return, present value of growing annuities, systematic withdrawal plans, annuities, bucket strategies, sustainable withdrawal rates and managing sequence risk. When revising, practise corpus and SIP calculations step by step, understand the trade-off between guaranteed income and flexibility, and know how to structure income from multiple sources.
questions: A client needs ₹10 lakh in the first year of retirement, rising 6% a year, for 20 years, withdrawn at the start of each year. If the corpus earns 8%, the required corpus is closest to:
₹2.00 crore
₹1.06 crore
₹1.43 crore
₹1.68 crore
PV of a growing annuity due = 10 lakh × Σ (1.06/1.08)^t for t = 0 to 19 ≈ ₹1.68 crore. ₹2.00 crore ignores returns and ₹1.06 crore ignores inflation in withdrawals.
A client wants ₹50 lakh in 15 years through a monthly SIP. Assuming 12% a year (1% a month), the monthly SIP needed is closest to:
Monthly SIP = FV × r ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1) = 50,00,000 × 0.01 ÷ (1.01^180 − 1) ≈ ₹10,008. ₹27,778 simply divides the target by 180 months and ignores returns.
A retiree buys an annuity for ₹50 lakh at an annuity rate of 7% a year. Her annual annuity income is:
Annual annuity = purchase price × annuity rate = 50,00,000 × 7% = ₹3,50,000. This income is generally fixed and taxable as per slab, so it loses purchasing power over time.
A systematic withdrawal plan (SWP) from a mutual fund helps a retiree by:
Guaranteeing a fixed return for life
Providing regular cash flow while staying invested
Avoiding all taxes on withdrawals
Locking money in for ten years
An SWP redeems a set amount at intervals, offering regular income while the rest stays invested. Returns are not guaranteed, and each redemption may attract capital gains tax.
Sequence-of-returns risk is highest:
At the start of a career
When the corpus is very small
Just before and after retirement
Only for clients with annuities
Poor returns soon after withdrawals begin can permanently deplete the corpus, since units are sold at low prices. This makes the years around retirement the most vulnerable.
In a bucket strategy, the long-term bucket is usually invested in:
Growth assets such as equity
Savings bank account balances
Overnight funds only
Cash kept at home
The long-term bucket is meant for expenses many years ahead, so it can hold growth assets that beat inflation. Near-term buckets hold safe, liquid assets.
Compared with an annuity, an SWP-based retirement income plan offers:
A guaranteed income for life
Flexibility and access to capital
Protection from all market risk
Payments that never change
An SWP keeps capital accessible and can be adjusted, but income depends on market returns and the corpus can run out. Annuities give guaranteed lifelong income but lock in capital.
A retiree withdraws 10% of his corpus each year while it earns 7%. What is the main risk?
The corpus will grow without limit
His tax liability will fall to zero
Inflation will be eliminated
The corpus may run out early
Withdrawing more than the corpus earns, especially after inflation, depletes capital each year and can exhaust it well before death. A sustainable withdrawal rate is needed.

Income Tax Fundamentals.overview: This chapter covers the basics of Indian income tax for individuals: residential status, heads of income, the old and new tax regimes, deductions and exemptions, rebate, surcharge and cess, clubbing of income, set-off and carry forward of losses, advance tax and filing returns. The Income-tax Act, 2025 has replaced the 1961 Act from April 2026 with largely similar concepts, so focus on principles rather than section numbers, and use current slab and rebate figures only when sure of the year.
questions: A resident salaried individual opts for the new regime for FY 2025-26. Gross salary is ₹12,50,000 with no other income. After the standard deduction and rebate, his income tax is:
Nil
Taxable income = 12,50,000 − 75,000 standard deduction = ₹11,75,000, which is within the ₹12 lakh rebate limit for FY 2025-26, so tax becomes nil. ₹60,000 is the tax before rebate on ₹12 lakh.
Rent received from a house property let out by an individual is taxed under the head:
Income from other sources
Profits and gains of business
Income from house property
Capital gains

Rental income from buildings and land appurtenant is taxed as income from house property, with a standard deduction allowed on net annual value. It is not business income unless property letting is the business itself.
A father transfers money to his minor son, who earns interest on it. In whose hands is this interest usually taxed?
The parent with higher income
The minor son alone
Neither, as minors are exempt
The bank paying the interest
Income of a minor child is generally clubbed with the income of the parent whose income is higher, subject to small exemptions and exceptions such as income from the child's own skill.
Advance tax is payable by an individual when:
He is a senior citizen with only pension income
He files his return after the due date
His income is entirely agricultural
Estimated tax for the year exceeds a set threshold
Advance tax must be paid in instalments during the year if estimated liability exceeds the prescribed limit. Resident senior citizens without business income are exempt.
Which of the following is a capital asset under income tax law?
Listed shares held as investment
Stock-in-trade of a trader
Personal clothing worn by the owner
Agricultural land in a rural area
Investments such as listed shares are capital assets. Stock-in-trade, personal effects like clothing and specified rural agricultural land are excluded from the definition.
An individual is resident in India for a tax year if, among other conditions, he is in India for at least:
30 days in that year
365 days in that year
182 days in that year
90 days in each of the last ten years
Staying in India for 182 days or more in the year makes an individual resident. There is also an alternative 60-day plus 365-day test, with modifications for certain citizens.
Health and education cess on income tax is levied on:
Gross total income
Only salary income
Only capital gains
Tax plus surcharge
Cess of 4% is charged on the amount of income tax plus any surcharge, not on income directly. It applies across heads of income.
Under the old regime, a deduction for life insurance premium and PPF contributions is available up to an overall limit for:
Any expense on consumer goods
Specified savings and payments
Rent paid to parents only
Losses from share trading

The old regime allows a deduction for specified investments and payments such as PPF, ELSS, life premiums and principal repayment of home loans, up to an overall ceiling. It is not available in the new regime.

Taxation of Investment Products.overview: This chapter covers how different investment products are taxed for resident individuals: equity shares and equity-oriented funds, debt funds, bonds, bank deposits, small savings, ELSS, ULIPs, NPS, gold and real estate. Key ideas are holding periods for short and long-term gains, applicable rates, exemption thresholds, tax deducted at source and treatment of dividends and interest. Rates have changed recently, so check the year in each question and focus on structure: what is taxed, when, and under which head.
questions: A resident sells listed equity shares held for two years with a long-term gain of ₹2,00,000 in FY 2025-26, with no other gains. Ignoring cess, the tax is:
Long-term gains on listed equity above ₹1,25,000 are taxed at 12.5%: (2,00,000 − 1,25,000) × 12.5% = ₹9,375. ₹25,000 wrongly taxes the whole gain at 12.5%.
Short-term capital gains on listed equity shares sold after 23 July 2024 are taxed at:
Slab rate
The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 raised the STCG rate on listed equity and equity-oriented funds, where STT is paid, from 15% to 20% for transfers on or after 23 July 2024.
Interest on a bank fixed deposit is taxed for an individual:
At a flat 10% as capital gains
At slab rates under other sources
Only when the deposit matures
Not at all if below ₹10 lakh
FD interest is income from other sources taxed at slab rates, usually on an accrual basis each year. Banks deduct TDS above thresholds, but TDS is not the final tax.
Which investment gives tax-free interest and maturity proceeds for an individual?
Public Provident Fund
Bank recurring deposit
Corporate non-convertible debentures
Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme
PPF is in the exempt-exempt-exempt category: interest and maturity amounts are tax-free. Interest on RDs, NCDs and SCSS is taxable at slab rates.
Units of a debt mutual fund bought in 2024 are sold after three years at a gain. How is the gain taxed?
At 12.5% as long-term gains
At 20% with indexation
Fully exempt after three years
At slab rates, irrespective of holding period
For specified funds with up to 35% in equity, units bought on or after 1 April 2023 have gains taxed at slab rates regardless of holding period, with no indexation.
On sale of a residential house, what is the holding period after which the gain is long-term?
More than 12 months
More than 24 months
More than 36 months
More than 60 months
Immovable property such as a house is a long-term capital asset if held for more than 24 months. Listed shares need more than 12 months.
Dividends received by a resident individual from Indian companies are:
Fully exempt
Taxed at 10% flat
Taxable at slab rates
Taxed only in the company's hands
Since the abolition of dividend distribution tax from April 2020, dividends are taxable in the hands of shareholders at their slab rates, with TDS above a threshold.
Sovereign gold bonds held until maturity give investors:
Exemption on redemption gains
Taxable gains at 30% on redemption
Tax-free interest every year
A deduction for the purchase cost
Capital gains on redemption of SGBs at maturity are exempt for individuals. The annual interest is taxable at slab rates, and there is no deduction on purchase.

Wealth Management & Estate Planning Conc.overview: This chapter introduces wealth management for high-net-worth clients and the basics of estate planning: ways of transferring wealth, nomination versus inheritance, joint holding, gifts, powers of attorney, wills and trusts, and the importance of documentation and record keeping. When revising, understand the different roles of nominee, legal heir, executor and trustee, how various tools fit different family situations, and why estate planning is part of every financial plan, not only for the very wealthy.
questions: Under the Companies Act, a nominee of shares receives the shares on the holder's death. According to the Supreme Court, the nominee:
Becomes the absolute owner in all cases
Must sell them within one year
Has no right to receive them
Holds them for the legal heirs
The Supreme Court has held that nomination does not override succession laws; the nominee receives the securities but holds them for the legal heirs or will beneficiaries.
A client holds a bank account jointly with 'either or survivor' mandate. On his death, the bank will:
Freeze the account until a probate is obtained
Pay the surviving joint holder
Transfer the balance to the government
Pay only the legal heirs named in a will
With an either-or-survivor mandate, the survivor can operate the account and receive the balance. The survivor may still hold it for heirs under succession law.
Which document lets a person appoint someone to manage his financial affairs while he is alive?
Will
Probate
Power of attorney
Succession certificate
A power of attorney authorises an agent to act on the principal's behalf during his lifetime. A will operates only after death, and probate and succession certificates are court documents.
Why is keeping an updated list of assets, accounts and policies important in estate planning?
It helps heirs trace and claim assets
It reduces the income tax rate payable
It replaces the need for a will
It is required to open a demat account
Heirs often struggle to locate assets, leading to unclaimed deposits and policies. A clear record speeds up transmission and reduces disputes.
Which is a common objective of wealth management for an HNI family?
Avoiding all forms of investment risk
Holding only cash in savings accounts
Maximising the number of bank accounts
Preserving and transferring wealth across generations
Wealth management integrates investment, tax, risk and estate planning to grow, protect and pass on wealth. Avoiding all risk or holding only cash would erode real value.
A gift of money from a father to his daughter is:
Taxable as her income above ₹50,000
Exempt in her hands, as she is a relative
Taxable in the father's hands at 30%
Prohibited under Indian law

Gifts received from specified relatives, including parents, are not taxable in the recipient's hands. However, income later earned on certain gifts may be clubbed in specific cases, such as gifts to a spouse.
Estate planning for a client with a child having special needs often uses:
A trust to manage assets for the child
Only a joint bank account with the child
A nomination in favour of a minor sibling
No planning, as courts will decide
A trust can provide professional management and ongoing support for a dependent who cannot manage money, with clear instructions on use of funds.
An executor of a will is responsible for:
Writing the will on behalf of the testator
Challenging the will in court
Carrying out the will's instructions
Collecting income tax from the heirs
The executor administers the estate after death: collecting assets, paying debts and distributing property as per the will, and may apply for probate where needed.

Wills, Succession & Trusts.overview: This chapter covers the law and practice of wills, intestate succession and trusts in India. It includes the requirements of a valid will, codicils, revocation, probate and letters of administration, succession under the Hindu Succession Act, the Indian Succession Act and Muslim personal law, and the creation and types of trusts under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. When revising, practise distributing an estate under intestacy rules and know the roles of settlor, trustee and beneficiary.
questions: A testator wants to make a small change to his existing will without rewriting it. He can do so through a:
Probate
Codicil
Succession certificate
Trust deed
A codicil is a document that alters, explains or adds to a will and must be executed like a will. Probate and succession certificates are court documents.
Is registration of a will compulsory in India?
Yes, an unregistered will is void
Only for wills of senior citizens
Only if the estate exceeds ₹1 crore
No, it is optional
Registration of a will is optional; an unregistered will is valid if properly executed and attested. Registration can, however, help prove authenticity.
A Hindu male dies intestate leaving his widow, two sons and his mother. Under the Hindu Succession Act, his self-acquired property is shared:
Only between the two sons
Half to the widow and half to the sons
Equally among all four
Entirely to the mother
Widow, sons and mother are all Class I heirs and take equal shares, so each gets one-fourth. Daughters, if any, would also share equally.
A trust in which the trustee has discretion over how much each beneficiary receives is a:
Discretionary trust
Specific trust
Public charitable trust
Revocable will
In a discretionary trust, beneficiaries' shares are not fixed and the trustee decides distributions. In a specific (determinate) trust, shares are fixed in the deed.
Under the Indian Trusts Act, the person who holds and manages trust property for others is the:
Settlor
Beneficiary
Trustee
Executor
The trustee holds legal title and manages property for beneficiaries as per the trust deed. The settlor creates the trust and the beneficiary enjoys the benefit.
A will is automatically revoked when:
The executor dies before the testator
The testator makes a later will revoking it
A witness to the will changes address
The testator's property rises in value
A will can be revoked by a later will or codicil, or by destroying it with intent to revoke. The executor's death or a witness moving does not revoke it.
Which court document is generally needed by heirs to collect debts and securities of a deceased person who left no will?
Probate
Codicil
Power of attorney
Succession certificate
A succession certificate authorises heirs to collect debts and securities of an intestate deceased. Probate applies to a will, and a power of attorney ends at death.
A 'living trust' created by a client during his lifetime can help by:
Avoiding probate and managing assets
Increasing his income tax rate
Cancelling all his nominations
Making his assets public records
A trust holds assets during life and after death per the deed, so the assets pass without probate and can be managed continuously. It also offers privacy.

Comprehensive Financial Planning & Case.overview: This chapter brings together all topics into comprehensive financial plans for clients. It covers gathering data, analysing the current position, prioritising goals, integrating insurance, investments, retirement, tax and estate planning, presenting recommendations and reviewing the plan. Case-study questions test judgement: what to address first, how to resolve conflicting goals and what to change when circumstances shift. When revising, practise full calculations and focus on logical, client-centred recommendations.
questions: A 35-year-old client has no life insurance, ₹5 lakh credit card debt and plans to start equity SIPs. What should come first?
Starting equity SIPs of the full surplus
Buying a second home with a loan
Investing in a new fund offer
Clearing the card debt and buying term cover
Protecting dependants and eliminating expensive debt come before long-term investing. Card interest far exceeds expected investment returns, and lack of cover exposes the family.
A client needs ₹30 lakh for a goal in 4 years. Which allocation is most suitable?
Entirely in small-cap equity funds
Entirely in a sector fund
Mostly debt with limited equity
Entirely in cryptocurrency
Short horizons leave little time to recover from equity falls, so most of the money should be in debt, with only limited equity exposure if any.
A married couple has a child. Which change should trigger an immediate plan review?
A routine rise in the index
The birth of the child
A change in the bank's branch timings
A new mobile phone
A new dependant changes insurance needs, cash flows, goals and estate plans. Routine market moves do not by themselves require a full plan review.
A client has two goals competing for limited surplus: a car in two years and retirement in 25 years. A sensible approach is to:
Fund retirement and size the car goal to fit
Ignore retirement until the car is bought
Take a large loan for both goals
Put all savings into the car goal
Long-term needs like retirement benefit from early saving, so they should not be neglected. The discretionary goal can be scaled down or delayed to fit the budget.
A client in the highest tax bracket asks for a debt option. Which factor is most relevant to compare?
Pre-tax returns only
Post-tax returns
The colour of the brochure
The number of branches of the issuer
For high-bracket clients, tax treatment can change rankings significantly, so comparison should be on post-tax, risk-adjusted returns.
A financial plan's recommendations are presented to the client. What should follow?
Locking the plan with no changes ever
Selling all existing investments at once
Implementation and periodic monitoring
Sending the plan only to the bank
After agreement, the plan is implemented and regularly monitored and revised. Plans must adapt to changes; wholesale selling may cause unnecessary costs.
A client's education goal costs ₹15 lakh today and is 10 years away. At 8% education inflation, the future cost is closest to:
₹32.4 lakh
₹27.0 lakh
₹15.0 lakh
₹40.0 lakh
Future cost = 15 lakh × 1.08^10 ≈ ₹32.4 lakh. ₹27.0 lakh uses simple growth of 8% a year, which understates compounding inflation.
Which action best shows client-centred advice in a case where the client is risk-averse but needs higher returns for a goal?
Push him into high-risk products without discussion
Promise him high returns with low risk
Ignore the goal and plan only for tax
Discuss trade-offs like saving more or delaying
When risk tolerance and required return conflict, the adviser should explain options such as increasing savings, extending the timeline or revising the goal, rather than ignoring the conflict.

Securities Markets and Their Role.overview: This chapter explains why securities markets exist and how they work: channelling savings into investment, price discovery, liquidity and risk sharing. It introduces the main participants and intermediaries, including issuers, investors, stock exchanges, clearing corporations, depositories, brokers and depository participants, and the regulators SEBI and RBI. When revising, be clear about who does what in the market, the difference between primary and secondary markets, and how market infrastructure protects investors.
questions: Which of the following is a market infrastructure institution in the Indian securities market?
A mutual fund distributor
An investment adviser
A listed company
A stock exchange

Stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories are market infrastructure institutions that provide core trading, clearing and holding systems. Distributors, advisers and issuers use this infrastructure.
How do securities markets help the economy grow?
By moving savings to productive businesses
By fixing the prices of all goods and services
By printing money for companies
By guaranteeing returns to all savers
Securities markets let companies and governments raise funds from savers for productive investment. They do not fix goods prices, print money or guarantee returns.
Liquidity in a securities market means that investors can:
Get guaranteed profits on every trade
Buy or sell quickly at fair prices
Hold securities only in physical form
Avoid paying any transaction costs
A liquid market has many buyers and sellers, so trades can be executed quickly without large price impact. Liquidity does not guarantee profits or remove costs.
A depository participant (DP) acts as:
The regulator of stock exchanges
The issuer of new shares
The investor's link to the depository
A bank that lends to listed companies
DPs, such as banks and brokers, open demat accounts and offer depository services as agents of NSDL or CDSL. SEBI is the regulator and companies are issuers.
Which regulator oversees stock brokers and stock exchanges in India?
RBI
SEBI
IRDAI
PFRDA
SEBI regulates stock exchanges, brokers, depositories and other securities market intermediaries. RBI regulates banks and money markets, IRDAI insurance and PFRDA pensions.
Investors in the securities market include:
Only banks and insurance companies
Only the central government
Only listed companies
Individuals, institutions and foreign investors
Investors range from retail individuals and HUFs to mutual funds, insurers, pension funds and foreign portfolio investors. Diversity of participants adds depth to the market.
Price discovery in the secondary market happens through:
A price set by SEBI every morning
The issuer announcing a daily price
Interaction of buy and sell orders
The depository fixing a price
Prices emerge from the matching of many buy and sell orders on the exchange, reflecting available information and demand and supply. No authority fixes daily prices.
Which is an example of a financial security?
A corporate bond
A residential flat
A tonne of wheat
A painting
Securities are tradable financial instruments such as shares, bonds and units. Flats, commodities and art are physical assets, not securities.

Securities, Asset Allocation and Investi.overview: This chapter covers the types of securities available to investors, including equity, preference shares, bonds, hybrids and mutual fund units, along with the risks and returns of each. It introduces asset allocation, diversification and the basics of investing, such as return measures, the power of compounding, inflation and investment approaches like fundamental and technical analysis. When revising, compare securities by risk and return, and understand why asset allocation matters more than picking individual securities.
questions: An investor buys a share at ₹200 and sells it after a year at ₹230, receiving no dividend. What is her return?
Return = (230 − 200) ÷ 200 = 15%. 13% wrongly divides the gain by the selling price, and 30% is the rupee gain, not a percentage.
Which security typically offers the highest potential return along with the highest risk?
Government treasury bills
Bank fixed deposits
Equity shares
AAA-rated corporate bonds
Equity holders are residual claimants, so returns are uncertain but potentially high. Treasury bills, deposits and top-rated bonds pay fixed amounts with lower risk.
A company has a P/E ratio of 25 and EPS of ₹16. What is its share price?
Price = P/E × EPS = 25 × 16 = ₹400. The other options add the numbers or divide them, which misapplies the definition of the P/E ratio.
Why does inflation matter to investors?
It increases the face value of bonds
It reduces the real value of returns
It guarantees higher share prices
It has no effect on savings
Inflation erodes purchasing power, so returns must be judged after inflation. A deposit earning less than inflation loses real value.
Technical analysis mainly studies:
A company's balance sheet
Past prices and volumes
Management quality
Industry growth prospects
Technical analysts study price and volume charts to identify trends and patterns. Fundamental analysts examine financial statements, management and industry prospects.
An investor with a 3-year goal and low risk appetite should give most weight to:
Debt instruments
Small-cap shares
Equity derivatives
Sector funds
Short horizons and low risk tolerance call for stable instruments such as deposits and debt funds. Small caps, derivatives and sector funds are volatile.
₹1 lakh invested at 10% compounded annually becomes how much after 3 years?
FV = 1,00,000 × 1.1³ = ₹1,33,100. ₹1,30,000 is the simple-interest value, which ignores interest earned on interest.
A bond's coupon rate is:
The price at which it trades
Its yield to maturity
The rating given by an agency
The interest rate on its face value
The coupon rate is the annual interest paid as a percentage of face value. YTM depends on the market price, and ratings measure credit quality.

Primary Markets.overview: This chapter covers how companies raise money by issuing securities to investors: public issues (IPOs and FPOs), rights issues, preferential allotments, QIPs, bonus issues and private placements. It explains book building and fixed price issues, price bands, investor categories, ASBA and UPI, allotment, listing and the roles of intermediaries such as lead managers and registrars. When revising, learn the steps of a public issue and who may bid in each category.
questions: In a fixed price issue, investors know:
Only a price band before applying
The issue price before applying
The price only after listing
Nothing about the price until allotment
In a fixed price issue the price is stated in the offer document before bidding. In a book-built issue only a price band is known and the final price is set after bidding.
A bonus issue means that a company:
Sells new shares to the public at a discount
Buys back shares from shareholders
Gives free shares to existing holders
Issues debentures to banks
A bonus issue capitalises reserves into free shares for existing shareholders. It raises no fresh money and does not change each holder's proportionate stake.
Which investors can apply in the anchor investor portion of an IPO?
Qualified institutional buyers
Retail individual investors
Employees of the issuer only
Non-resident individuals only
Anchor investors are QIBs who apply for a large minimum amount a day before the issue opens, giving price confidence. Retail investors bid in their own category.
Who decides the final issue price in a book-built issue?
SEBI
The stock exchange
The retail investors' association
The issuer with the lead managers
After bids close, the issuer and book running lead managers determine the final price within the band based on demand. SEBI does not set prices.
A company allots shares to a select group of investors, such as a strategic partner, on a non-public basis. This is a:
Rights issue
Bonus issue
Initial public offer
Preferential allotment
A preferential allotment issues shares to specific persons, subject to ICDR pricing and lock-in rules. A rights issue goes to all existing holders pro rata.
What does the term 'oversubscribed' mean for an issue?
Bids exceed the shares on offer
Fewer bids than shares on offer
The issue was cancelled by SEBI
Shares listed below the issue price
An issue is oversubscribed when demand exceeds supply; allotment is then made as per the basis of allotment, with retail investors often receiving the minimum lot by lottery.
Before investing in an IPO, an investor should read the:
Company's advertisements only
Offer document's risk factors
Social media posts on the IPO
Grey market premium updates
The offer document gives detailed information including risk factors, financials and objects of the issue. Advertisements and social media are not a substitute.
Which intermediary handles applications, allotment and refunds in a public issue?
Credit rating agency
Custodian
Registrar to the issue
Stock broker
The registrar processes applications, finalises allotment with the exchange and coordinates unblocking or refunds. Rating agencies, custodians and brokers have other roles.

Secondary Markets.overview: This chapter explains how listed securities are traded: stock exchanges, trading members, order types, the trading session, market and limit orders, circuit filters, clearing and settlement, margins, contract notes and investor protection. When revising, learn the trading cycle from order to settlement, how different orders behave, why margins are collected, and the protections available to investors, including grievance redressal and investor protection funds. Settlement timelines and charges change over time, so focus on the process.
questions: An investor places a market order to buy 100 shares. This order will:
Execute only at a price he specifies
Execute at the best available price
Remain pending until the next day
Be cancelled if the price moves
A market order executes immediately at the best price available in the order book. A limit order executes only at the specified price or better.
Pay-out in the settlement process means:
Investors pay money to the exchange
Brokers collect margins from clients
The exchange cancels unsettled trades
Buyers get securities and sellers get funds
Pay-out is when the clearing corporation delivers securities to buyers and funds to sellers. Pay-in is when buyers pay funds and sellers deliver securities.
A price band on an individual stock limits:
How far its price can move in a day
The number of shares that can be bought
The brokerage that can be charged
The dividend the company can pay
Price bands or circuit filters restrict the daily price range of a stock to curb excessive volatility. They do not limit quantities, brokerage or dividends.
An investor buys 50 shares at ₹400 and sells them at ₹380. Ignoring charges, his loss is:
Loss = (400 − 380) × 50 = ₹1,000. ₹20 is the loss per share, not the total.
Why should an investor check the contract note received from his broker?
To verify trade details and charges
To find the next day's market trend
To claim dividends from the company
To change his demat account number
The contract note confirms price, quantity, time and charges for each trade, helping investors detect errors or unauthorised trades quickly.
Which service lets investors file and track complaints against listed companies and intermediaries online?
RBI Retail Direct
NSDL e-voting
SEBI SCORES
AMFI's NAV page
SCORES is SEBI's online complaint redress system, linked to market-wide dispute resolution. Retail Direct is for G-secs, e-voting for shareholder resolutions and AMFI's page for NAVs.
A stop-loss sell order is typically used by an investor who:
Wants to buy only when prices fall
Wants to limit losses if prices fall
Wants to ensure the highest selling price
Wants to avoid any execution at all
A stop-loss sell order becomes active when the price falls to a trigger, helping cap losses on a holding. It does not guarantee the best price.
The role of the clearing corporation in the secondary market is to:
List new companies on the exchange
Hold investors' securities in demat form
Fix brokerage rates for all brokers
Guarantee settlement of trades
The clearing corporation clears and settles trades and guarantees settlement through novation, removing counterparty risk. Depositories hold securities.

Mutual Funds.overview: This chapter introduces mutual funds for securities market learners: the concept of pooling, the trust structure, NAV, types of schemes (equity, debt, hybrid, index and ETFs), open and closed-ended schemes, SIPs, costs such as expense ratio and exit loads, and investor rights. When revising, compute NAV and units, understand how passive and active funds differ, and learn how to choose a scheme based on goals, horizon and risk shown in the riskometer.
questions: An investor invests ₹10,000 in a scheme at a NAV of ₹25. How many units does she get, ignoring charges?
250 units
400 units
2,500 units
40 units
Units = amount ÷ NAV = 10,000 ÷ 25 = 400. The other options misplace the decimal or divide the wrong way.
An exchange traded fund differs from a regular open-ended index fund because ETF units:
Are bought only from the AMC at day-end NAV
Carry guaranteed returns
Have no expense ratio at all
Trade on a stock exchange during market hours
ETF units are listed and traded on exchanges at market prices throughout the day. Open-ended index fund units are bought and redeemed with the AMC at NAV.
Who appoints the asset management company of a mutual fund and oversees it on behalf of unitholders?
The trustees
The custodian
The registrar
The distributor
Trustees protect unitholders' interests, appoint the AMC with SEBI approval and monitor its compliance. Custodians hold assets and registrars maintain records.
A closed-ended scheme:
Allows purchases and redemptions daily with the AMC
Has no maturity date at all
Has a fixed maturity and lists units
Can be bought only by companies
Closed-ended schemes accept money only during the NFO, have a fixed term and list units on exchanges for liquidity. Open-ended schemes allow continuous transactions.
Which fund type aims to match an index's return rather than beat it?
Small-cap fund
Index fund
Focused fund
Value fund
Index funds are passively managed and replicate an index, aiming for returns close to it at low cost. Active funds try to outperform their benchmarks.
A balanced advantage fund mainly aims to:
Hold only government bonds
Invest only in gold
Track a single sector index
Shift between equity and debt dynamically
Balanced advantage (dynamic asset allocation) funds change their equity and debt mix based on market conditions or valuation models.
Which statement about mutual fund returns is correct?
They are not guaranteed
They are guaranteed by SEBI
They are fixed at the time of NFO
They are insured by DICGC
Mutual fund returns depend on the performance of underlying investments and are not guaranteed. DICGC insurance covers bank deposits, not fund units.
A scheme's NAV fell from ₹40 to ₹36 over a year with no payouts. The return is:
Return = (36 − 40) ÷ 40 = −10%. −11.1% divides by the ending NAV, and −4% is the rupee change per unit.

Derivative Markets.overview: This chapter introduces derivatives traded in Indian markets: forwards, futures and options, their underlying assets (equity, indices, currencies, commodities and interest rates), key terms such as lot size, expiry, premium, strike and open interest, and how they are used for hedging, speculation and arbitrage. It also covers margins and the risks of leverage. When revising, compute simple futures and option payoffs, understand settlement types, and learn why derivatives can magnify both gains and losses.
questions: A trader buys a call with a strike of ₹200 for a premium of ₹8. At expiry the stock is at ₹215. What is the net profit per share?
Payoff = 215 − 200 = ₹15; net profit = 15 − 8 = ₹7. ₹15 ignores the premium paid.
An investor buys one futures lot of 500 shares at ₹300 and sells it at ₹310. Ignoring costs, her profit is:
Profit = (310 − 300) × 500 = ₹5,000. ₹10 is the profit per share; multiplying by lot size gives the total.
The maximum loss for an option buyer is:
Unlimited
The premium paid
The strike price
Twice the premium
An option buyer can let the option lapse, so the most he can lose is the premium. Option sellers face larger potential losses.
A put option buyer profits when the underlying price:
Rises above the strike price
Stays exactly at the strike
Rises above strike plus premium
Falls below strike minus premium
A put gains when the underlying falls; net profit starts below strike minus premium. Rising prices hurt a put buyer.
Index futures in India are settled at expiry by:
Cash settlement
Physical delivery of all index stocks
Delivery of an ETF
Rolling over automatically
An index cannot be delivered, so index futures and options are cash settled based on the final settlement price.
A rise in open interest along with rising prices usually suggests:
Short sellers closing positions
No trading activity
New long positions being added
The contract has expired
Rising open interest with rising prices typically indicates fresh buying. Short covering usually reduces open interest while prices rise.
Why do derivatives carry high risk for small investors?
They are not regulated by SEBI
Their prices never change
They cannot be sold before expiry
Leverage magnifies losses
Derivatives require only margin for large exposure, so small price moves cause large losses relative to capital. They are regulated and can be closed before expiry.
A company that will import goods in three months buys currency futures to fix its rupee cost. It is:
Speculating
Hedging
Arbitraging
Market making
Using derivatives to offset an existing business exposure is hedging. Speculation takes positions without an underlying exposure.

Basics of Derivatives.overview: This chapter introduces derivatives across asset classes covered in the common derivatives exam: equity, currency, interest rate and commodity. It explains forwards, futures, options and swaps, exchange-traded versus OTC contracts, the participants (hedgers, speculators, arbitrageurs) and the economic functions of derivatives. It also traces how derivatives markets developed in India. When revising, focus on definitions, the differences between contract types, and the benefits and risks of derivatives for different users.
questions: Which of the following derivatives is usually traded over the counter rather than on an exchange?
Nifty index futures traded on the NSE
USD/INR exchange-traded options
A currency swap between two companies
Gold futures on a commodity exchange
Swaps are customised bilateral contracts, generally traded OTC. Index futures, exchange-traded currency options and commodity futures are standardised exchange products.
A rice exporter sells USD forward to protect against rupee appreciation. Her role is that of a:
Hedger
Speculator
Arbitrageur
Market maker
She has a genuine foreign currency exposure and uses a forward to offset it, which is hedging. Speculators take positions without an underlying exposure.
Which feature makes derivatives useful for transferring risk?
They remove risk from the economy entirely
Risk passes to those willing to bear it
They guarantee profits to both parties
They can be used only by banks
Derivatives move price risk from hedgers to speculators or other hedgers with opposite exposures. Total risk in the economy is not eliminated.
An option differs from a futures contract because the option buyer:
Has an obligation to buy or sell at expiry
Pays no money at the start
Faces unlimited losses
Has a right but not an obligation
An option buyer pays a premium for the right to exercise, with no obligation. Futures bind both parties, and option buyers' losses are limited to the premium.
Commodity derivatives on Indian exchanges are now regulated by:
The Forward Markets Commission
SEBI
The RBI
The Ministry of Consumer Affairs
The Forward Markets Commission merged into SEBI in 2015, and SEBI now regulates commodity derivatives exchanges and brokers along with securities markets.
Arbitrage in derivatives markets helps by:
Increasing price differences between markets
Removing the need for any regulation
Guaranteeing that prices always rise
Keeping related prices in line
Arbitrageurs exploit price gaps between related markets; their trades push prices back into alignment, improving market efficiency.
Which risk is a key concern in OTC derivatives but much lower in exchange-traded ones?
Price risk on the underlying
Changes in interest rates
Counterparty default risk
Volatility of the underlying

Exchange trades are guaranteed by a clearing corporation through novation and margins. OTC deals rely on the counterparty's creditworthiness, though central clearing has reduced this for some products.
The underlying of an interest rate futures contract in India is typically:
A government security or interest rate
A basket of listed equity shares in the Nifty
A tonne of steel
A foreign currency pair
Interest rate futures are based on government bonds or reference rates, letting users hedge interest rate risk. Equity, commodity and currency futures have other underlyings.

Introduction to the Underlying Markets.overview: This chapter covers the cash markets that underlie the derivatives in this exam: equity markets and indices, the foreign exchange market and currency quotes, the government securities and money markets, and physical commodity markets. Learn how prices are quoted in each, what drives them, how indices are built, how forex quotes and cross rates work, and how bond prices relate to yields. When revising, practise cross-rate and yield calculations and understand the main participants and regulators of each market.
questions: EUR/USD is 1.08 and USD/INR is 84.00. What is the implied EUR/INR rate?
EUR/INR = EUR/USD × USD/INR = 1.08 × 84.00 = 90.72. Dividing instead gives 77.78, which is the wrong direction for this cross.
In the quote USD/INR = 84.00, the base currency is:
INR
USD
Both equally
Neither, it is a cross rate
In a pair quoted as A/B, A is the base currency and the price shows how many units of B buy one unit of A. Here one USD costs 84 rupees.
If the rupee depreciates against the dollar, the USD/INR rate will:
Fall
Remain unchanged
Become negative
Rise
Depreciation means more rupees are needed to buy one dollar, so USD/INR increases, for example from 84 to 85.
Spot gold is ₹72,000 per 10 g and the near-month futures price is ₹72,900. The basis (spot minus futures) is:
Basis = spot − futures = 72,000 − 72,900 = −₹900. A negative basis indicates futures trading above spot, as in a contango market.
Who conducts auctions of government dated securities and treasury bills on behalf of the Government of India?
SEBI
Reserve Bank of India
NSE
Clearing Corporation of India
The RBI manages public debt and conducts primary auctions of G-secs and T-bills. CCIL clears and settles trades in these securities.
Which factor is most likely to strengthen the rupee against the dollar?
A sharp rise in India's oil import bill
Large outflows by foreign portfolio investors
Large foreign capital inflows into India
Higher inflation in India than in the US
Capital inflows increase demand for rupees, supporting its value. Higher imports, outflows and higher relative inflation tend to weaken the rupee.
When market interest rates rise, the prices of existing government bonds generally:
Fall
Rise
Stay the same
Double
Bond prices move inversely to yields. Existing bonds with lower coupons become less attractive when new bonds offer higher rates, so their prices fall.
A physical commodity market differs from the equity market because commodity prices are strongly affected by:
Company quarterly earnings
Dividend announcements
Share buyback decisions
Weather, harvests and global supply
Agricultural and other commodity prices depend on supply factors like weather, crop size, inventories and global demand. Earnings and dividends drive equity prices.

Introduction to Forwards and Futures.overview: This chapter covers forward and futures contracts across equity, currency, interest rate and commodity markets. It explains contract features, pricing using cost of carry and interest rate parity, convenience yield for commodities, basis, contango and backwardation, mark-to-market and final settlement. When revising, practise fair-value and forward premium calculations, understand how carrying costs and income affect pricing in each asset class, and know how settlement differs across contracts.
questions: A USD/INR futures contract has a lot size of USD 1,000. A trader buys one lot at 84.50 and sells it at 84.80. Ignoring costs, his profit is:
Profit = (84.80 − 84.50) × 1,000 = ₹300. The rate rose 30 paise per dollar on a 1,000-dollar contract.
USD/INR spot is 84.00 and the six-month forward is 85.26. The annualised forward premium is about:
Premium = (85.26 − 84.00) ÷ 84.00 = 1.5% for six months; annualised = 1.5% × 2 = 3.0%. 1.5% is the unannualised figure.
Convenience yield in commodity futures refers to:
The benefit of holding the physical good
Brokerage charged by the exchange
Interest earned on margin money kept with the broker
Profit made by a speculator
Convenience yield is the benefit to users of holding physical stock, such as avoiding production disruption. It can push futures prices below full cost of carry.
In a contango market, futures prices are:
Lower than spot prices
Equal to spot prices at all times
Not linked to spot prices
Higher than spot prices
Contango means futures trade above spot, usually reflecting carrying costs. Backwardation is the reverse, often due to supply shortages or high convenience yield.
Under interest rate parity, if Indian interest rates are higher than US rates, the USD/INR forward will trade at:
A discount to spot
Exactly the spot rate
Zero
A premium to spot
The currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount, so the dollar trades at a forward premium against the rupee. This offsets the interest differential.
Physical delivery of a commodity futures contract means that at expiry:
The seller delivers the commodity to the buyer
Only price differences are paid in cash
The contract is rolled over automatically to the next month
The exchange buys the commodity
In physically settled contracts, sellers deliver the actual commodity meeting quality norms at designated warehouses, and buyers pay the settlement value.
Why must a futures trader maintain a margin account?
To earn guaranteed interest
To cover daily losses
To pay dividends on the underlying
To pay the full contract value at expiry
Initial margin and daily mark-to-market ensure losses are settled every day, protecting the clearing corporation. It is not a savings or dividend account.
Interest rate futures prices rise when:
Bond yields rise
Inflation expectations rise sharply
Bond yields fall
The RBI raises the repo rate
IRF prices track bond prices, which rise when yields fall. Rate hikes and higher inflation expectations usually push yields up and IRF prices down.

Strategies Using Futures.overview: This chapter covers practical strategies with futures: hedging long and short exposures, beta-adjusted hedging of equity portfolios, currency hedging by exporters and importers, interest rate hedging, cash-and-carry and reverse arbitrage, calendar spreads, inter-commodity spreads and pair trading. When revising, identify whether a user should buy or sell futures for a given exposure, compute the number of contracts needed, and understand the risks that remain, such as basis risk.
questions: A portfolio worth ₹60 lakh has a beta of 1.5. Each index futures contract is worth ₹15 lakh. How many contracts should be sold for a full hedge?
Contracts = value × beta ÷ contract value = 60 × 1.5 ÷ 15 = 6. Ignoring beta gives 4, which would leave the portfolio under-hedged.
An importer who must pay USD in three months fears a rising USD/INR. He should:
Sell USD/INR futures
Buy USD/INR futures
Buy INR call options from a friend
Wait and buy dollars later
Buying USD/INR futures locks in the rupee cost of dollars. If the rupee weakens, futures gains offset the higher cost of buying dollars.
Basis risk in a hedge arises because:
The exchange may close permanently
Margins are not required in exchange-traded futures
Spot and futures may not move identically
Futures prices never change
If the hedged asset and the futures contract do not move in exact step, the hedge is imperfect. This basis risk remains even with the correct number of contracts.
A trader buys near-month gold futures and sells far-month gold futures. This is a:
Inter-commodity spread
Protective put
Covered call
Calendar spread
A calendar spread takes opposite positions in the same commodity across different expiries, profiting from changes in their price difference.
A bond portfolio manager expects interest rates to rise. To hedge, he should:
Buy interest rate futures
Buy more long-term bonds
Do nothing, as bonds rise with rates
Sell interest rate futures
Rising rates lower bond and IRF prices, so a short IRF position gains and offsets portfolio losses. Buying futures or bonds would increase exposure.
A trader buys crude oil futures and sells natural gas futures expecting their price relationship to change. This is:
An inter-commodity spread
A calendar spread
A cash-and-carry arbitrage
A naked short position
Positions in two related commodities aim to profit from changes in their relative prices. Calendar spreads use the same commodity at different expiries.
An investor holding shares worth ₹30 lakh wants to raise market exposure temporarily without buying more shares. She can:
Sell index futures
Sell her shares
Buy index futures
Buy put options on the index
Buying index futures adds market exposure with only margin. Selling futures, selling shares or buying puts would reduce exposure.
An exporter hedges USD receivables by selling USD/INR futures. If the rupee weakens sharply instead, the exporter will:
Gain on both the futures and the dollar receivables
Lose on futures but gain on receivables
Lose on both futures and receivables
Be unaffected on both positions
A weaker rupee raises the rupee value of receivables but causes losses on short futures. The hedge locks in a rate, giving up gains from favourable moves.

Introduction to Options.overview: This chapter covers options on equity, currency, commodity and interest rate underlyings: calls and puts, buyers and sellers, strike, premium, expiry, moneyness, intrinsic and time value, exercise styles and settlement. It introduces option pricing factors and the Greeks: delta, gamma, theta, vega and rho. When revising, practise payoff calculations for each position, understand how volatility and time affect premiums, and know how options on different underlyings are settled in India.
questions: A USD/INR call option has a strike of 84.00 and the spot is 84.75. Its intrinsic value is:
Zero
Call intrinsic value = spot − strike = 84.75 − 84.00 = ₹0.75 per dollar. It is positive because the call is in the money.
Theta of a long option position measures:
Change in value as volatility rises
Change in value as interest rates rise
Loss in value as time passes
Change in delta as price moves
Theta is time decay, the fall in an option's value as expiry approaches, other factors constant. Vega relates to volatility and rho to interest rates.
A put option with strike ₹1,000 and premium ₹30 is bought. At expiry the stock is at ₹1,050. The buyer's net result per share is:
Gain of ₹50
Loss of ₹30
Loss of ₹80
Gain of ₹20
The put expires worthless because the stock is above the strike, so the buyer loses only the premium of ₹30.
A call option's delta of 0.5 means that for a ₹1 rise in the underlying, the option price rises by about:
Delta measures the change in option price for a one-unit change in the underlying. A delta of 0.5 implies about ₹0.50 change, typical for at-the-money calls.
Which option is out of the money?
A call with strike above spot
A call with strike below spot
A put with strike above spot
A put with strike equal to spot
A call is OTM when strike exceeds spot, as exercise would mean buying above market. A put with strike above spot is in the money.
An option that can be exercised only on the expiry date is called:
American style
Bermudan style
Asian style
European style
European options can be exercised only at expiry, which is the style used for exchange-traded options in India. American options can be exercised any time before expiry.
Which factor increases the premium of both calls and puts?
Lower volatility of the underlying
Higher volatility of the underlying
Shorter time to expiry
A drop in market liquidity only
Higher volatility raises the chance of large moves, benefiting option holders, so both call and put premiums rise. Shorter time to expiry reduces premiums.
The seller of a put option receives the premium and is obliged to:
Sell the underlying at the strike if exercised
Pay the premium back at expiry
Buy the underlying at the strike if exercised
Deliver a call option to the buyer
A put gives its buyer the right to sell; the put writer must buy at the strike if exercised. Call writers have the obligation to sell.

Option Trading Strategies.overview: This chapter covers option strategies for different market views: buying and writing calls and puts, covered calls, protective puts, bull and bear spreads, straddles, strangles, butterflies, collars and ratio spreads, along with their use in currency and commodity markets. When revising, compute maximum profit, maximum loss and break-even points, match strategies to views on direction and volatility, and understand the risk of strategies with short options.
questions: A trader sells a ₹500 call at ₹14 and buys a ₹520 call at ₹5, same expiry. What is his maximum profit per share?
This bear call spread earns a net credit of 14 − 5 = ₹9, the maximum profit if the stock ends below ₹500. Maximum loss is 20 − 9 = ₹11.
A trader expects a big move in a stock after results but is unsure of direction. Which strategy fits?
Short straddle
Covered call
Long straddle
Bull call spread
A long straddle (buy call and put at the same strike) profits from a large move either way. A short straddle profits only if the price stays still.
A long strangle differs from a long straddle because the strangle:
Uses different out-of-the-money strikes
Uses the same strike for call and put
Involves selling both options
Has unlimited risk
A long strangle buys an OTM call and OTM put, making it cheaper than a straddle but needing a bigger move to profit. Both have limited risk.
An exporter expecting USD inflows buys a USD/INR put option. This protects him against:
A rise in USD/INR
A fall in USD/INR
Rising interest rates
Higher brokerage
A put gains if USD/INR falls, offsetting lower rupee value of his dollar receipts, while letting him benefit if the rupee weakens.
A trader buys one ₹100 call, sells two ₹110 calls and buys one ₹120 call. His maximum profit occurs if the stock ends at:
This is a long call butterfly, which peaks at the middle strike of ₹110 and has limited loss on either side.
Which strategy is suitable for an investor who is mildly bullish and wants to reduce the cost of buying a call?
Long put
Bear put spread
Short call alone
Bull call spread
A bull call spread buys a lower-strike call and sells a higher-strike call, reducing cost while capping upside. Puts and bear spreads are bearish.
A short straddle carries which risk?
Loss limited to the premium paid
Loss only if the price stays still
Large losses on big moves either way
No risk, as premiums are received
Selling a call and a put at the same strike earns premium but loses heavily if the price moves sharply in either direction.
An investor holds a stock and sells an OTM call on it to earn income. If the stock rises sharply, she will:
Miss gains above the strike
Lose more than the stock's rise
Receive unlimited profits
Lose the premium received
A covered call caps upside at the strike, as she must deliver the stock if assigned. She keeps the premium but gives up further gains.

Trading, Clearing, Settlement & Risk Man.overview: This chapter covers the operational framework for exchange-traded derivatives: trading systems, order types, membership categories, position limits, clearing and settlement through clearing corporations, mark-to-market and final settlement, margining and risk management including the settlement guarantee fund. It also covers settlement of currency, interest rate and commodity contracts. When revising, understand who settles with whom, how margins work, and why clearing corporations are central to managing default risk.
questions: A futures position worth ₹12 lakh requires an initial margin of 10%. How much initial margin is needed?
Initial margin = 10% × ₹12,00,000 = ₹1,20,000. ₹12,000 is 1% of the value, which misplaces the decimal.
In the derivatives segment, a self-clearing member clears and settles:
Trades of all other members
Only trades in the cash segment
Trades of foreign exchanges
Only its own and its clients' trades
A self-clearing member clears its own proprietary and client trades. A professional or general clearing member can clear trades of other trading members.
Exchange-traded currency futures in India are settled:
By physical delivery of US dollars
In cash in Indian rupees
In gold at the exchange vault
Through the RBI's forex reserves
Currency futures on Indian exchanges are cash settled in rupees; no foreign currency is delivered. Settlement is based on the FBIL reference rate at expiry.
A client's open position exceeds the client-level position limit. What is the likely consequence?
The exchange increases the limit for him
His broker's licence is automatically cancelled
Penalties and required reduction
Nothing, limits are only advisory
Exchanges levy penalties and require positions above limits to be reduced. Limits are binding and monitored to prevent concentration.
Why do clearing corporations conduct daily mark-to-market settlement of futures?
To generate extra revenue for members
To set the next day's opening price
To decide which stocks enter the index
To stop losses piling up
Settling gains and losses daily keeps exposures small and lowers default risk. MTM is not a revenue tool or a price-setting mechanism.
If a client fails to pay a margin call, the broker may:
Ask the exchange to waive the margin
Close out the client's position
Transfer the loss to another client
Extend the deadline indefinitely
Brokers can square off positions of clients who fail to meet margin calls, to limit losses. Using other clients' funds is prohibited.
Novation in exchange-traded derivatives means:
The exchange cancels all trades at day end
Brokers trade only with their own clients
The clearing corporation is counterparty to all
SEBI approves each trade individually
Through novation, the clearing corporation interposes itself as buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer, guaranteeing settlement.
Extreme loss margin is charged in addition to initial margin to cover:
Losses beyond normal risk estimates
Brokerage and stamp duty
Losses only on expiry day
Taxes payable on profits
Extreme loss margin covers losses in situations beyond those captured by the initial margin model, adding a further buffer for the clearing corporation.

Legal and Regulatory Environment.overview: This chapter covers the legal and regulatory framework for equity, currency, interest rate and commodity derivatives in India: the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, the SEBI Act, FEMA and RBI directions for currency and interest rate derivatives, and the integration of commodity market regulation into SEBI. It also covers rules on participants, position limits and market abuse. When revising, know which regulator governs which aspect, why currency derivatives involve both SEBI and RBI, and how regulators curb manipulation.
questions: Exchange-traded currency derivatives in India are jointly governed by:
SEBI and the RBI
IRDAI and PFRDA
Only the Ministry of Commerce
Only the stock exchanges
Currency derivatives fall under FEMA, administered by the RBI, while exchanges and brokers are regulated by SEBI. Hence both regulators issue directions.
Which law governs foreign exchange transactions, including the use of currency derivatives by residents?
Companies Act, 2013
Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015 and the Insurance Act
Indian Partnership Act, 1932
FEMA regulates foreign exchange dealings; RBI frames rules under it for currency derivatives. The other laws concern companies, insurance and partnerships.
A commodity broker must register with:
FMC
RBI
SEBI
NABARD
After the FMC merged with SEBI in 2015, commodity derivatives brokers are registered and regulated by SEBI like other stock brokers.
Spreading false rumours to move the price of a futures contract for personal gain is:
A permitted trading strategy
Allowed if done on social media
Only an ethical concern with no penalty
A fraudulent practice punishable by SEBI
Spreading false information to influence prices is prohibited under SEBI's rules against fraudulent and unfair trade practices and can attract penalties.
SEBI imposes position limits on derivatives mainly to:
Prevent concentration and manipulation
Guarantee profits to small traders
Increase brokerage income
Fix the price of derivatives
Position limits stop any single participant from dominating a contract, reducing manipulation and default risk.
Who frames the regulations on margins, position limits and contract design for exchange-traded derivatives?
Each client individually
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs
Credit rating agencies
SEBI, with exchanges implementing them
SEBI sets the framework, and exchanges and clearing corporations implement contract specifications, margins and limits within it.
An entity wants to act as a clearing member in the derivatives segment. It must:
Only open a bank account
Get approval from the RBI alone
Meet net worth norms and be registered
Only be a listed company
Clearing members must meet SEBI and clearing corporation criteria, including net worth and deposits, and be registered. Listing or a bank account alone is insufficient.
Insider trading rules apply to derivatives because:
Derivatives are not regulated by SEBI
Their prices depend on the underlying
Only cash market trades can be manipulated
Insiders are barred only from mutual funds
Trading derivatives on unpublished price-sensitive information gives the same unfair advantage as trading shares, so insider trading regulations cover them.

Accounting and Taxation.overview: This chapter covers the accounting and tax treatment of derivatives across asset classes. It includes accounting for margins, mark-to-market, premiums and open positions under accounting standards, the treatment of hedge accounting, the classification of derivatives income for tax, Securities Transaction Tax on equity derivatives and Commodity Transaction Tax on commodity derivatives, and stamp duty. Rates change through Finance Acts, so focus on what each tax applies to, who pays it and how income is classified.
questions: Commodity Transaction Tax (CTT) is levied on:
Purchase of physical agricultural goods
Currency futures trades
Sale of non-agricultural commodity derivatives
Equity cash market trades
CTT applies to taxable commodity derivatives, mainly non-agricultural contracts, on the seller. Currency derivatives do not attract STT or CTT.
Under Ind AS, hedge accounting allows a company to:
Match hedge and hedged-item results
Avoid recording derivatives in books
Show derivatives only at cost
Postpone all losses indefinitely
Hedge accounting aligns recognition of gains and losses on the hedging instrument with those on the hedged item, reducing artificial volatility in profit.
For an individual, income from trading currency derivatives on a recognised exchange is generally treated as:
Speculative income
Exempt income
Long-term capital gain
Non-speculative business income
Eligible derivatives traded on recognised exchanges, including currency derivatives, are excluded from speculative transactions and treated as non-speculative business income.
Do exchange-traded currency futures attract Securities Transaction Tax?
Yes, on the buyer
No
Yes, on both parties
Only on expiry day
STT applies to securities transactions such as equity and equity derivatives. Currency derivatives are not covered by STT.
At year-end, an open futures position with an unrealised loss is accounted for by:
Ignoring it until the position is closed
Adding it to share capital
Recognising the loss in the accounts
Treating it as a gain
Accounting standards require derivatives to be measured at fair value, so MTM losses on open positions are recognised. Prudence does not allow ignoring them.
Premium received by an option writer on an open position is initially shown as:
Income immediately
A liability until expiry or exercise
Share capital
A fixed asset
The premium received is held as a liability because the writer still has an obligation. It is recognised as income when the option expires or is closed.
Losses from F&O trading treated as non-speculative business can be carried forward for up to:
Two years
Four years
Indefinitely
Eight years
Non-speculative business losses can be carried forward for eight assessment years to be set off against business income, provided the return is filed on time.
Stamp duty on derivatives trades in India is collected:
Through exchanges, from the buyer
By SEBI from the seller
By the RBI from banks
By the depository from issuers
Stamp duty on securities transactions, including derivatives, is collected centrally by exchanges or clearing corporations from the buyer and passed to states.

Sales Practices, Code of Conduct & Inves.overview: This chapter covers ethical selling and investor protection for derivatives across asset classes: suitability and risk disclosure, KYC, code of conduct for brokers and their representatives, handling of client funds and securities, avoiding mis-selling and unauthorised trades, and grievance redressal through exchanges, SCORES and online dispute resolution. When revising, focus on practical scenarios: what a broker should say or do, what is prohibited, and how a client can seek redress.
questions: A broker's employee advises a first-time client to put all his savings into commodity futures because 'prices only go up'. This is:
Mis-selling and a code breach
Good advice for a new investor
Permitted if the client agrees
Required to increase market liquidity
Recommending highly leveraged products without suitability assessment and with false claims is mis-selling and breaches the code of conduct.
A client notices trades in his account that he did not authorise. His first step should be to:
Ignore it if the trades made profit
Wait for the year-end statement
Complain to the broker at once
Close his bank account
Clients should raise unauthorised trades immediately with the broker and escalate to the exchange or SCORES if unresolved. Delay can weaken the claim.
Brokers must give clients a risk disclosure document mainly to:
Advertise new products
Collect personal data for marketing
Guarantee returns
Explain the risks of trading
The risk disclosure document informs clients of leverage, potential losses and other risks before trading, enabling informed decisions.
Why should a broker not accept cash from clients for margins?
Cash is never accepted anywhere in India
Rules require traceable banking channels
Cash payments lower the margin needed
Cash is safer than bank transfers
SEBI norms require client funds to be received through banking channels from the client's own account for traceability and to prevent misuse.
A broker shares a client's trading details with another client without consent. This breaches:
Confidentiality obligations
Position limits
Price band rules
Margin rules
Brokers must keep client information confidential except where law or consent permits disclosure. Sharing with other clients is a breach.
Which platform offers online conciliation and arbitration for disputes between investors and market intermediaries?
The Insurance Ombudsman
The Consumer Affairs helpline
SEBI's ODR portal
The Income Tax portal
SEBI's Online Dispute Resolution platform handles conciliation and arbitration of securities market disputes, including derivatives, after initial complaint routes.
Before trading derivatives, a client must be assessed for:
His preferred news channel
Suitability and financial capacity
His favourite sports team
His social media followers
Brokers must assess whether the client has adequate financial capacity and understanding, often through income proof, before enabling derivatives.
A broker uses one client's credit balance to meet another client's margin shortfall. This is:
Allowed if both are related
A standard netting practice
Required by exchange rules
Prohibited misuse of client funds
Client funds must be used only for that client's obligations. Using them for another client is misuse and attracts strict action.

Introduction to Research Analyst Profess.overview: This chapter introduces the research analyst's role in capital markets: types of analysts (sell-side, buy-side, independent), the research process, the skills required, and how research supports investors, fund managers and companies. It also covers the ethical foundations of the profession: independence, objectivity, managing conflicts and protecting confidential information. When revising, understand who uses research, how analysts add value, and why independence from investment banking and trading interests is so important.
questions: An independent research firm sells reports to institutional investors and has no broking or banking business. Its main advantage is:
Guaranteed accuracy of forecasts
Access to insider information
Fewer conflicts of interest
Exemption from SEBI regulation
Without broking or investment banking revenue, independent research faces fewer pressures to be positive on clients' stocks. It is still regulated and cannot use inside information.
Which skill is most essential for an equity research analyst?
Designing company logos
Operating a trading terminal for clients
Selling insurance policies
Analysing financial statements
Analysts must interpret financial statements, model earnings and value businesses. Design, dealing and insurance sales are different professions.
A buy-side analyst at a mutual fund mainly produces research for:
Retail clients of a broker
The fund's own portfolio managers
The company being analysed
The general public through newspapers
Buy-side research supports internal investment decisions of the fund. Sell-side research is distributed to clients of brokers and banks.
Why do analysts follow a structured research process?
To make conclusions consistent and well supported
To ensure every report ends with a buy rating on the stock
To avoid reading company disclosures
To meet a quota of reports each day
A structured process of data gathering, analysis, valuation and review helps produce objective, defensible recommendations. It does not dictate ratings.
A company management offers an analyst a free foreign holiday ahead of a results briefing. The analyst should:
Decline it to protect independence
Accept it and publish a positive report
Accept it if the report is delayed
Accept it and share it with colleagues
Accepting valuable gifts from covered companies compromises objectivity. Analysts should decline such benefits or follow strict firm policies on modest hospitality.
Which is a key way research analysts add value to markets?
Fixing share prices for exchanges
Guaranteeing returns to investors
Improving price discovery
Approving IPO documents for SEBI
By analysing information and publishing views, analysts help prices reflect fundamentals. They do not set prices, guarantee returns or approve offer documents.
A sell-side analyst's report is most likely to be distributed to:
Only the analyst's family members
Only the board of directors of the company being covered
Only SEBI officials
The broker's institutional and retail clients
Sell-side research is produced by brokers and banks and distributed to their clients to support trading and investment decisions.
Professional scepticism in research means the analyst should:
Accept management guidance without any independent checks
Question management claims and verify them
Rely only on market rumours
Copy other analysts' estimates
Analysts should test management's statements against data, industry evidence and independent sources rather than accept them at face value.

Introduction to Securities Market.overview: This chapter covers the securities market from an analyst's perspective: primary and secondary markets, market participants, stock exchanges, clearing corporations, depositories, indices and the regulatory structure. It also covers market efficiency and the types of securities traded. When revising, understand how trading and settlement work, how indices are built, and how market structure affects liquidity and price discovery, since these influence how analysts interpret prices and volumes.
questions: A market where prices quickly reflect all publicly available information is called:
Weak form efficient only, not semi-strong
Strong form efficient
Semi-strong form efficient
Inefficient

Semi-strong efficiency means public information is rapidly priced in, so fundamental analysis of public data alone should not give consistent excess returns. Strong form also includes private information.
Which participant provides liquidity by quoting both buy and sell prices?
A market maker
A depository
A registrar
A credit rating agency
Market makers stand ready to buy and sell, narrowing spreads and improving liquidity. Depositories hold securities, registrars keep records and rating agencies assess credit.
Why do analysts watch trading volumes along with prices?
Volume decides the company's dividend
Volume fixes the face value of shares
Volume is the same as market cap
Volume shows the strength of a move
A price move on high volume suggests broad participation and conviction; low-volume moves may be less reliable.
Market capitalisation of a company equals:
Face value × shares outstanding
Share price × shares outstanding
Total assets − total liabilities
Net profit × P/E of the index
Market cap is the market value of all outstanding shares. Face value times shares is paid-up capital, and assets minus liabilities is book value.
A sector index differs from a broad market index because it:
Includes every listed company
Is not based on prices
Is computed only once a year
Tracks stocks of one industry
Sector indices such as banking or IT indices track a single industry, helping analysts compare sector performance with the broader market.
Which is a primary market activity?
A company issuing new shares in an IPO
Two investors trading shares on NSE
A fund selling shares on BSE
A broker squaring off a client's trade
Primary market activity involves new securities issued by companies. Trading existing shares among investors is secondary market activity.
Who regulates the securities market in India?
RBI
SEBI
IRDAI
CCI
SEBI regulates exchanges, intermediaries, issuers' disclosures and research analysts. RBI handles banks and money markets, IRDAI insurance and CCI competition.
Why do analysts compare a stock's return with a benchmark index?
To set the stock's dividend
To decide the company's tax
To judge relative performance
To fix the index's base value
Comparing returns with a benchmark shows whether a stock outperformed or underperformed the market or sector, which helps judge recommendations.

Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets.overview: This chapter covers key terms analysts use in equity and debt markets: face value, book value, market price, EPS, dividend, payout ratio, P/E, earnings yield, market capitalisation, corporate actions, coupon, yield to maturity, current yield, duration, credit ratings and spreads. When revising, make sure you can compute and interpret each measure, understand how corporate actions affect per-share data, and know the relationship between bond prices, coupons and yields.
questions: A stock trades at a P/E of 25. What is its earnings yield?
Earnings yield = 1 ÷ P/E = 1 ÷ 25 = 4%. It expresses earnings as a percentage of price and is often compared with bond yields.
A company earns EPS of ₹20 and pays a dividend of ₹6 per share. What is its dividend payout ratio?
Payout ratio = DPS ÷ EPS = 6 ÷ 20 = 30%. The retention ratio is 70%, the share of earnings kept for reinvestment.
When a bond trades at a premium to face value, its YTM is:
Above its coupon rate
Equal to its coupon rate
Below its coupon rate
Always zero
Paying above face value lowers the effective return, so YTM is below the coupon. Discount bonds have YTMs above their coupons.
A rights issue at a price below market typically leads to:
An automatic rise in EPS for all existing holders
A fall in the share price ex-rights
An increase in face value
No change in share count
After the record date, the share price adjusts down because new shares are issued at a discount, diluting value per share. The share count rises.
Credit spread on a corporate bond is:
Its yield minus a comparable G-sec yield
Its coupon minus its face value
The difference between bid and ask prices
The rating agency's fee
The credit spread measures extra yield for credit and liquidity risk over a risk-free government security of similar maturity.
Book value per share is computed as:
Market price ÷ EPS
Net profit ÷ total assets
Shareholders' equity ÷ shares outstanding
Total debt ÷ total shareholders' equity on the balance sheet
Book value per share = net worth ÷ number of shares. Price ÷ EPS is the P/E, profit ÷ assets is ROA and debt ÷ equity is leverage.
Modified duration of a bond indicates:
The time until the next coupon
Price change for a 1% change in yield
The bond's credit rating
The number of coupons the bond pays in each year
